item.title: Jason Brennan goes for the jugular
item.description: Meet G.A. Cohen's harshest critic. Part 2 of 3 of a series on capitalism, socialism, and community.
item.content:encoded:
In Part 1, we looked at G.A. Cohen’s core objection to capitalism.

Today, we’ll consider a notable response.

Why Not Socialism? argues for socialist ideals using the parable of a camping trip. At the campground, we prefer to be among friends and equals. It would be desirable to make society more like that, says Cohen, even though we don’t yet know any feasible way to run the economy on friendly vibes, as opposed to the “fear and greed” of capitalism.

There’s something charming about this. But it’s a “tepid defense,” says Heath. What kind of socialist won’t even come out and tell you socialism works?

Share

Why Not Capitalism?

Say what you will about Jason Brennan: nobody has ever described him as “tepid.” The arguments of Why Not Capitalism? are more in the style of “guns blazing,” or “dirty bomb aimed at jugular vein.” For example:

Cohen’s ultimate legacy—the ultimate result of his life’s work defending socialism—will be to help us see that from a moral point of view, the intrinsically best society is capitalist. Cohen also became famous in part for criticizing the libertarian philosopher Robert Nozick. In Chapter 4, I’ll explain that another legacy of Cohen’s work will be to show that Nozick was basically right all along about the nature of utopia. (p. 24)

Even the cover art is a dunk:

Personally, I liked teaching this book alongside Cohen’s. Brennan makes a number of interesting points that are worth any student’s time.

For example, Brennan argues that Cohen’s use of “camping trip” stacks the deck against capitalism. Cohen lovingly describes all the good things about his socialist version of the trip—bonhomie, sharing, etc.—but none of the downsides. When he imagines the more capitalist camping trip, he does the opposite, focusing on greed and fear. Brennan calls this the “the essential flaw” of Why Not Socialism?: instead of comparing ideal socialism to ideal capitalism, or nonideal socialism to nonideal capitalism, Cohen compares ideal socialism to nonideal capitalism.1

To even the odds, Brennan presents a capitalist spin on Cohen’s camping trip—the Mickey Mouse Clubhouse Village. In this idyllic community, the villagers share some facilities but also enjoy their own private spheres. They all “cooperate with a common desire that everyone have the freedom and resources to flourish under their own conceptions of the good life” (p. 26). Some villagers work for others—like Daisy Duck at Minnie Mouse’s Bowtique—but wages are fair, and the workplace is respectful. Villagers do their part, have fun when work’s done, act with extreme kindness, and accept one another’s differences. It’s a utopia. To “reinforce” that point, Brennan invites you to consider an alternative Clubhouse where the villagers act like socialists. Donald murders millions of people as he forcibly nationalizes the farmland. Goofy throws dissenters in the gulag. Minnie’s “five-year plans” wreck the economy. Mickey installs himself as Premier for life. It’s dystopia of coercion and deprivation.

Why is the capitalist Clubhouse Village more attractive? Brennan highlights five principles:

  1. Voluntary Community: Everyone lives together without threats of violence.

  2. Mutual Respect: People tolerate each other and value diversity.

  3. Reciprocity: Each has something to offer to society, and people take pride in being able to exchange value for value.

  4. Social Justice: Nobody has to live an indecent life, thanks to the norms of trade and property rights, inter alia.

  5. Beneficence: Everyone is motivated to help those in need.

Now, there are three types of objections you might have to this list.

First, you might deny that these principles—however nice they sound in the abstract—are really so desirable to realize in society. For example, anti-liberals might argue that mutual respect is bad when some people hold views that aren’t worthy of respect. Should we tolerate totalitarian ideologies? “Harmful” views about gender? Would you value a diversity of opinions about whether the Jews caused 9/11?2

Second, you might grant the goodness of the principles while denying that they are characteristic of capitalism. In a review, Dan Iley-Williamson contends that all of Brennan’s principles are compatible with socialism. Even if that’s not right, readers may wonder: why should any sort of social justice be essential to, or even compatible with, capitalism?

There’s something right about this challenge. But let me try to stick up for Brennan a little here, since I think he’s making an underrated point. When we talk about the basic legal institutions of capitalist societies—property law, contract law, criminal law, etc.—we’re usually critiquing them. (If not just taking them for granted.) But it’s at least arguable that these institutions are, in part, the legacy of historic moral victories. To see what I mean, consider a pre-modern struggle over contracts—the saga of the colleganza in medieval Venice. The colleganza was a type of arrangement between an investor and a traveler: the investor would fund a trading voyage, the traveler would actually go on said voyage, and afterwards the two would split the profits. Of course, any Marxist would call this division of labor exploitative—why should the rich guy who stays home get to make any money? But at the time, the colleganza was seen as a threat to idle rich guys, since it gave enterprising commoners a path to nobility and prosperity.3 Puga and Trefler (2014) argue that political elites responded to the colleganza by cracking down and installing a very different set of legal institutions, designed to entrench the incumbent elites—a disaster for both community and equality.

…starting in 1297, a small group of particularly wealthy merchants blocked political and economic competition: they made parliamentary participation hereditary and erected barriers to participation in the most lucrative aspects of long-distance trade. Over the next two centuries this led to a fundamental societal shift away from political openness, economic competition, and social mobility and toward political closure, extreme inequality, and social stratification.

In sum, it’s an interesting question whether Brennan’s principles are all desirable and all capitalist, but even if we disagree with him, we shouldn’t go overboard, caricaturing market institutions as—always and everywhere—pure fear-and-greed machines designed by wealthy elites. Sometimes the elites are the ones trying to constrain markets, either to protect themselves from competition or prevent commoners from climbing up. It’s worth remembering that our modern legal system is, in some important respects, an inclusive institution worth preserving.

Subscribe now

Finally, you might find yourself thinking, this whole Mickey Mouse style of argument is ridiculous! Brennan is just stuffing all the good stuff he likes into this community and calling it capitalist. How does that prove that capitalism is morally superior? Fair question! But did you ask the same about Cohen’s camping trip? The styles of argument are, by design, quite similar. (Of course, you might think that neither argument is persuasive, but then the socialist isn’t going to get much juice out of Cohen.)

Fraternité bros

Now for my favorite part of Brennan’s book, which has to do with community and equality. Recall that, for Cohen, community requires more than warm fuzzy feelings. It may require us to redistribute people’s just holdings, since inequality makes it impossible for us to relate to one another as fellows.

We cannot enjoy full community, you and I, if you make, and keep, say, ten times as much money as I do, because my life will then labor under challenges that you will never face, challenges that you could help me to cope with, but do not, because you keep your money. (p. 35)

Cohen illustrates with a lovely example: the bus-rider and the car-driver.

I am rich, and I live an easy life, whereas you are poor, because of regrettable choices and/or bad option luck, and not, therefore because of any lack of equality of opportunity. You have to ride the crowded bus every day, whereas I pass you by in my comfortable car. One day, however, I must take the bus, because my wife needs the car. I can reasonably complain about that to a fellow car-driver, but not to you. I can’t say to you: “It’s awful that I have to take the bus today.” There is a lack of community between us of just the sort that naturally obtains between me and the fellow car-driver. And it will show itself in many other ways, for we enjoy widely different powers to care for ourselves, to protect and care for offspring, to avoid danger, and so on. (pp. 35–6)

In short: we need equal incomes, or else we’ll live in what Tom Nagel once called “essentially ununifiable worlds.” For Cohen, that means bye bye, community.

But does economic inequality always undermine communal relatability? Brennan has his doubts. Think of communities based on a shared hobby—Brennan’s example is guitar geeks. Or consider the kinds of communities that can exist within an academic hierarchy.

As a graduate student, I had little difficulty being in community with my advisors, though they made at least ten times my income. Despite these differences, we had and have much stronger community with one another than we do with many others who have identical wealth. (p. 126)

I think Brennan’s point is a fair one. Cohen underrates the possibility of being in community with people who aren’t your equals.4

How could the socialist respond? They might concede that community is possible when there are relatively small income differences. But can any ordinary person be in community with a centi-billionaire? Forget the car: what about private jets? Private space shuttles? Private companies building space shuttles? Private mega-bunkers across the globe?

Maybe Cohen’s principle of community gets its revenge when we think of wealth on a larger scale.5

Pluralism and liberté

But Brennan has one more trick up his sleeve—pluralism. If differences undermine community, it won’t be enough to equalize incomes. What if we have different religious beliefs? Different values, tastes, and aspirations? Isn’t it bad to stamp out diversity, and perverse to do it in the name of community? Brennan thinks so, illustrating with a “Borg Camping Trip.”

Like Star Trek’s Borg Collective, everyone is the same. There are no differences in taste, values, appearance, mannerism, talents, skills, behaviors, preferences, ideas, beliefs, ethnicity, religion, lifestyle, and dreams. After all, they reason, the more distinct they are from each other, the harder it is for them to understand or empathize with each other, and so the harder it is for them to maintain community. (p. 120)

Brennan finds this “repugnant”: community is just “one value among many,” and the Borg Camping Trip maximizes it until it “destroys everything else that matters.”

One way to think of this is as a symptom of Cohen’s own lack of pluralism, specifically in his theory of values. Yes, he has equality and community—égalité and fraternité, as they were called during the French Revolution. But what about the Revolution’s other value? Whatever happened to liberté?6

Subscribe now

Conclusion

If you’ve just read Cohen for the first time, I can easily recommend Brennan as a next step. Right-leaning students will get their first taste of a lot of important ideas—like the leveling-down objection. Left-leaning students will confront all sorts of provocative questions—like “Do we really need equality in order to have community?”7

But we’re not done yet. In Part 3, we’ll encounter one of the decade’s most ambitious attempts at philosophical jiu-jitsu—a dense, demanding paper full of high-proof insights about cooperation and human nature. We’re taking a cold, hard look at ’s argument that, for creatures like us, in large societies like ours, Cohen’s own principle of community is best realized by none other than his arch-nemesis: market capitalism.

Will Joe pull the rabbit out of the hat—or will the magic trick fall flat?

1

Cohen’s argument involved a kind of cheating, but I doubt Cohen realized he was cheating. Cohen probably thought there was no need to compare ideal capitalism to ideal socialism, because he thinks that “ideal capitalism” is an oxymoron—you know, like “business ethics” or “military intelligence.” (p. 77)

2

Relatedly, are we sure that Brennan-style reciprocity is desirable? Granted, many people do take pride in “having something to offer.” And social science does seem to indicate that, as puts it, “market competition is pro-social” in some important sense. But people also are outraged by so-called “price gouging”—e.g. jacking up the prices of water after a hurricane, or hand sanitizer during a pandemic—which is just market reciprocity at work. This point, too, has been consistently supported by social scientific findings. In the words of Nobel laureate Richard Thaler, “Basically, it just isn’t socially acceptable to raise prices in an emergency.”

3

For example, Patrisse Cullors, co-founder of the Black Lives Matter Movement, has advocated abolishing the court system. In An Abolitionist’s Handbook (p. 8), Cullors writes:

Abolition centers on getting rid of prisons, jails, police, courts and surveillance. Period.

“No courts, period” is a bold proposal. Cullors is, by any reckoning, one of the most influential activists in the world. Why has there been so little discussion of her take on the legal system? Do people think we can have social justice in a world without any courts? Maybe they assume she doesn’t mean it?

4

Consider also on masculine hierarchies:

Placement in a male hierarchy, explicit or otherwise, is the mark of success in cultivating one’s masculinity. And here’s the thing progressives miss: being at the bottom is okay. In healthy male hierarchies everyone has a role to play and gets respect if they do it well. The guy riding the bench on the football team is still on the team. The only thing that’s unacceptable is being kept outside of the hierarchy entirely. That’s rejection of you as a man, not being accepted at the bottom. Progressive attempts to abolish hierarchies run counter to men’s instincts and also create structures in which men don’t know how to function.

What do you think a left egalitarian like Cohen—or like Liz Anderson—should say in response?

(Yes, of course, they could point to particular examples where hierarchies go wrong. But that doesn’t make the problem go away: some communities depend on hierarchy, and it’s not obvious what to do about that fact. Abolish those communities? Do harm reduction? Just suck it up and live with the badness? Surely some especially immoral hierarchies should be abolished, such as what Blight calls the “slave society” of the antebellum South. But every hierarchy? (Are we abolishing high school prom, the Super Bowl, the Billboard Hot 100, Substack leaderboards, etc.?) For more, see on status inequalities and Joe Heath, “Egalitarianism and Status Hierarchy,” Chapter 3 of Cooperation and Social Justice.)

5

At some point, however, I think the Cohenite socialist is going to have to go beyond relatability to talk about other aspects of community, like “thin trust” (which even unequal societies might have in spades) and “the dark side of social capital” (e.g. suffocating obligations to share with kin and friends, greater familial control over marriage and work, increased racial conflict due to “bonding social capital” within groups, ritualized inculcations of loyalty).

Sadly there isn’t a big knob on top of human society with “COMMUNITY” written on it—and even if there were, cranking it up might stir up energies that Cohen would rather leave dormant. It’s worth remembering that when George Orwell was trying to persuade England to go socialist, he appealed primarily to patriotism—not exactly the go-to value of American socialists. For example:

That’s the DSA’s Darializa Avila Chevalier, Democratic nominee for NY’s 13th district. When pressed about the deleted tweet, she didn’t exactly take it back.

To be clear, I’m not saying anything about whether patriotism and nationalism are good. I’m just saying there’s a tension between thinking patriotism is cringe, as many contemporary socialists do, and basing your socialism in love of community, as Cohen does. In the 21st century, the most potent communitarian force in the world is probably flag-waving, patriotic nationalism. Even people’s most heartfelt commitments to political principles—whether to socialism, liberalism, or democracy—don’t have the same resonance. When Ukrainians volunteer to fight in the fourth year of a deadly war, do you think they’re fighting for the timeless principles of liberal democracy? They’re fighting for Ukraine.

6

It’s interesting that, in the history of political philosophy, individual liberty and collective diversity have tended to go together. “Liberty upsets patterns,” Robert Nozick used to say. The main text of Friedrich Hayek’s The Constitution of Liberty literally ends on the word “diversity.” Edmund Burke goes the other way round: a “diversity of members and interests” helps secure a “general liberty.” Or just open On Liberty to a random page and behold.

These days, “diversity” is better known as the fading watchword of academic and corporate progressives, who prefer concepts like “systemic racism” to old-fashioned liberté. See, e.g., my discussion of academic DEI:

(Of course, diversity ain’t dead—read some Ryan Muldoon if you don’t believe me.)

7

For a more critical take on Brennan’s book, see e.g. Dan Iley-Williamson, who argues that Brennan doesn’t do enough to support free-market capitalism over the alternatives—like welfare-state capitalism and property-owning democracy—and contends that Brennan misreads Cohen at several points. (Thanks to for the pointer.)

Did I leave out your favorite objections to Brennan and Cohen? Remember: Substack sharing is solidaristic caring.

item.title: The best free resources for learning Philosophy, Politics, and Economics
item.description: Games, talks, courses, videos, and (of course) SEP entries.
item.content:encoded:
Inspired by ’s post on free philosophy lectures, I want to share some of my favorite free online resources for learning PPE—i.e., philosophy, politics, and economics, an interdisciplinary degree that’s been growing ever since it started in Oxford a century ago.

Share

Subscribe now

Note: I’ve tried to include a variety of sources, media, and viewpoints, but this is not a comprehensive list. Tell me in the comments what you think I’ve left out!1

Games

  • The Parable of the Polygons

    • Created by Vi Hart and Nicky Case, this game lets you play around with Thomas Schelling’s model of segregated neighborhoods. It’s a perfect way to see how micromotives cause macrobehavior.

  • The Evolution of Trust

    • Another Nicky Case gem—this time, based on Robert Axelrod’s Evolution of Cooperation. Probably the single best introduction to the Prisoner’s Dilemma that you can find online.

    • For more on the repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma with noise, see Axelrod’s follow-up The Complexity of Cooperation—in particular the material about “generosity” and “contrition.”

  • The Game of Life

    • The definitive zero-player game, John Conway’s Game of Life lets you see how self-sustaining patterns can emerge from extremely simple deterministic rules. Dan Dennett once said every philosopher should have to study it before they’re allowed to start writing.

Talks

  • Elinor Ostrom, “Beyond Markets and States”

    • This is the best version of Ostrom’s Nobel Prize lecture—a wonderful mix of theoretical and empirical insights about how people actually solve collective action problems.

    • For more on Ostrom, see Ashley Hodgson’s excellent videos.

  • Robert Putnam, “Bowling Alone”

    • A precursor to the classic book on community (aka social capital). This talk was five years before Bowling Alone turned Putnam from an academic “big deal” into an actual big deal. You can feel the electricity in the room as people realize they’re in the presence of something much bigger than your usual lecture.

  • , “Recent Advances in the Understanding of Human Sociality”

    • A romp through big ideas in the philosophy of social science.

  • Geoff Sayre-McCord on Adam Smith

    • Speaking of great speakers…

Subscribe now

Courses

  • Ian Shapiro, “Power and Politics”

    • If you subscribe to Big iff True, you knew this was coming. One of the greatest PPE courses ever taught. I especially recommend the lectures on money in politics, distributive politics, and 9/11.

    • See also my interview with Prof. Shapiro about After the Fall, his 2026 book based on this course.

  • Ian Shapiro, “Moral Foundations of Politics”

    • Not my fault the guy has two outstanding online courses. Don’t miss the lectures on Rawls, Burke, Locke, Nozick, and the “neoclassical synthesis” of rights and utility.

  • John Rawls, “Modern Political Philosophy”

    • Somebody needs to freshen up the audio and chuck in some metadata, but this is still an invaluable resource—a class on political philosophy from the most influential American political theorist of the last century, who was also a famously conscientious teacher.

  • David Blight, “The Civil War and Reconstruction”

    • My own view is that, if you want to study PPE, you should try to study at least a little history (and vice versa). Blight’s lectures on 19th-century America are a perfect case in point. You can’t possibly watch these without learning something about political power, ideology, and racism.

      • Bonus: Coates on Blight on Douglass.

    • Speaking of race in America, Clint Smith has a series of shorter videos on Black American History, several of which have great PPE themes: e.g. the vidoes on Women’s Experience under Slavery, Washington vs. Du Bois, and Frederick Douglass.

  • Marginal Revolution University

    • An extraordinary resource for econ essentials. Credit to and . Here are some playlists to get you started:

      • Micro

      • Macro

      • Econometrics

      • Supply & Demand

      • The Wealth of Nations (includes a chapter-by-chapter summary—invaluable if you’re about to read Smith)

Other videos

  • Veritasium on the Prisoner’s Dilemma and Arrow’s Theorem

  • Toby Handfield on Social Choice Theory

  • Ashley Hodgson

    • An underrated YouTube channel with tons of great economics explainers.

      • Nash equilibrium

      • Backwards induction and game trees

      • Prospect theory

  • Dan Bonevac, “Mill on Freedom of Speech”

    • My favorite conservative philosopher (and one of the most generous teachers I’ve ever met). Dan’s knowledge is astonishingly broad—not many channels have videos on Wittgenstein, Frege, Heidegger, Godel, Plato, and Aquinas. Below is his video on Mill on freedom of speech.

  • G.A. Cohen, “Against Capitalism”

    • The Marxist philosopher G.A. Cohen—about whom I’ve published a series of posts—lays out the objection that capitalism is unjust because of the forced expropriation of land.

  • Brian Leiter and Jamie Edwards, “Marx”

    • Based on their new book, which I found wonderfully clear and informative. There are also comments by Geoffrey Wodke and Steven Durlauf (who is also, by the way, an important contributor to the debate over social capital).

SEP entries

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy is the best free resource for learning philosophy—by far.

Here are a few pieces relevant to PPE that you might enjoy:

  • Exploitation

  • Feminist Political Philosophy

  • Kant’s Social and Political Philosophy

  • Rawls

  • Business Ethics

  • Philosophy of Economics

  • Democracy

  • The Free Rider Problem

  • Voting

  • War

Is there a free Substack I can subscribe to for more free PPE?

Funny you should ask…

item.title: Grieving for Tom Hill, a philosopher we need now more than ever
item.description: We've lost one of the greats: a deep thinker who wanted to know why humans matter, what makes us equal, and why we shouldn't be afraid of "a storm in the wilds."
item.content:encoded:
As human beings we are part of nature, living, growing, declining, and dying by natural laws similar to those governing other living beings; despite our awesomely distinctive human powers, we share many of the needs, limits, and liabilities of animals and plants. These facts are neither good nor bad in themselves, aside from personal preference and varying conventional values. To say this is to utter a truism which few will deny, but to accept these facts, as facts about oneself, is not so easy — or so common. Much of what naturalists deplore about our increasingly artificial world reflects, and encourages, a denial of these facts, an unwillingness to avow them with equanimity.

—Thomas E. Hill, Jr., “Ideals of Human Excellence and Preserving Natural Environments”

I woke up to some painful news today: the death of Thomas Hill, Jr.—one of the most admired moral philosophers of his time, and the author of one of the great papers of the 20th century, “Servility and Self-Respect.”

This is a huge loss for Tom’s family and loved ones, as well as for his many students (to whom he was devoted). It was also the loss of an important thinker, who had some quietly inspiring ideas about what made human life important—and, as a result, how we should feel about others and ourselves.

I take that back: “quietly inspiring” is too understated. No, Tom didn’t write in a grandiose style. He wasn’t polemical; he was anything but sensationalistic. But his moral philosophy was a profound challenge to our culture in 2020s—an era of looks-maxxing, vice-maxxing, people-shopping, defiantly unrestrained warfare, and fantasies of immortality.

Tom thought that ethics was in large part about our attitudes. Racist hatred, for example, is objectionable for the (obvious) reason that its target doesn’t deserve it. A human’s worth isn’t grounded in something as superficial as skin color; so, if you denigrate someone or their achievements purely on the basis of race, your attitudes involve a kind of moral distortion. But what made Tom’s work special is that he didn’t stop there. What, he asked, must the racists think of themselves? That they’re only worthy of love and respect because they happen to be of the right race? That is a kind of distortion, too—this time at the racist’s own expense. The racist who denigrates others also thereby denigrates the humanity in themselves.

In “Servility and Self-Respect,” Tom makes the same point in the opposite direction. The person who disrespects themselves is, in a way, disrespecting others, by virtue of missing what makes everybody matter. This paper features Tom’s best-known thought experiment, for which he will be remembered for many years: The Deferential Wife, who displays the vice of servility.

This is a woman who is utterly devoted to serving her husband. She buys the clothes he prefers, invites the guests he wants to entertain, and makes love whenever he is in the mood. She willingly moves to a new city in order for him to have a more attractive job, counting her own friendships and geographical preferences insignificant by comparison. She loves her husband, but her conduct is not simply an expression of love. She is happy, but she does not subordinate herself as a means to happiness. She does not simply defer to her husband in certain spheres as a trade-off for his deference in other spheres. On the contrary, she tends not to form her own interests, values, and ideals; and, when she does, she counts them as less important than her husband’s. She readily responds to appeals from Women’s Liberation that she agrees that women are mentally and physically equal, if not superior, to men. She just believes that the proper role for a woman is to serve her family. As a matter of fact, much of her happiness derives from her belief that she fulfills this role very well. No one is trampling on her rights, she says; for she is quite glad, and proud, to serve her husband as she does. (89)

Hill is careful here. The Deferential Wife might not be servile at all, depending on how we fill in the details. Maybe she was brainwashed and never had a way of knowing better? Maybe she can’t leave her husband and is making the best of a bad situation?1 Very possible. But it’s also possible that she simply doesn’t value herself enough—she may be serving her husband “just from laziness, timidity, or a desire for some minor advantage.” That, says Hill, is a moral defect. We shouldn’t let others walk all over us, even if standing up for ourselves requires a bit of effort and courage.

Nor does Hill stop there. Again, he asks, what kind of attitudes must this person have? In particular, think about how they must feel about others. The Deferential Wife is not some kind of subhuman species: she is a human being, with broadly the same cognitive, perceptual, and affective capacities as anybody else.2 If she isn’t worthy of basic respect, then nobody is.

Hill illustrates with another unforgettable example—the German dueling fraternity—though in my view, this example is massively underrated, because almost no philosophers have heard of it. In full:

Imagine a club, say, an old German dueling fraternity. By the rules of the club, each member has certain rights and responsibilties. These are the same for each member regardless of what titles he may hold outside the club. Each has, for example, a right to be heard at meetings, a right not to be shouted down by the others. Some rights cannot be forfeited: for example, each may vote regardless of whether he has paid his dues and satisfied other rules. Some rights cannot be waived: for example, the right to be defended when attacked by several members of the rival fraternity. The members show respect for each other by respecting the status which the rules confer on each member. Now one new member is careful always to allow the others to speak at meetings; but when they shout him down, he does nothing. He just shrugs as if to say, ‘Who am I to complain?’ When he fails to stand up in defense of a fellow member, he feels ashamed and refuses to vote. He does not deserve to vote, he says. As the only commoner among illustrious barons, he feels that it is his place to serve them and defer to their decisions. When attackers from the rival fraternity come at him with swords drawn, he tells his companions to run and save themselves. When they defend him, he expresses immense gratitude—as if they had done him a gratuitous favor. Now one might argue that our new member fails to show respect for the fraternity and its rules. He does not actually violate any of the rules by refusing to vote, asking others not to defend him, and deferring to the barons, but he symbolically disavows the equal status which the rules confer on him. If he ought to have respect for the fraternity, he ought to change his attitude. Our servile person, then, is like the new member of the dueling fraternity in having insufficient respect for a system of rules and ideals. The difference is that everyone ought to respect morality whereas there is no comparable moral requirement to respect the fraternity. (100)

In “Social Snobbery and Human Dignity,” Tom makes a similar point about people who respect only elites and high-achievers. After a winsome disclosure of the author’s own “strong personal aversion to snobbery, extreme enough to raise worries about ‘reverse snobbery’,” he goes on to argue that the snob’s attitudes betray a similar moral error as can be found in the servile person and the racist:

the main fault in snobbery is not error in judging the merits of individuals but rather failure to acknowledge the basic worth of human beings as persons. (156)

by measuring the worth of persons entirely by the variables of social class and/or individual merit, snobs fail to appreciate their own unconditional worth as persons. (157)

The essential error of the chauvinist of any stripe is to place the value of a human life in trifling and superficial things—refined taste, gender or race, etc.—rather than the deep fact that unites us: our shared humanity, the ability we each have to set our own goals and shape our own values, rather than responding heteronomously to our environments like mindless robots or natural slaves.

As I read Tom, he was in awe of the value of humanity—its value as an end in itself, he would surely add—and his touchstone for this was the work of Immanuel Kant. But I think it would be a grave mistake to pigeonhole Tom Hill as a “Kantian,” as if he were a disciple, less original than his contemporaries. To see Hill’s work—on humanity, duties to self, supererogation—as a mere footnote to one of the greats would be an injustice.

Hill was a great ethicist, which means that he has something important to tell us about coping with life and death. I began with a passage from his paper about humanity and nature, where Hill talks about the importance for humans of self-acceptance—not just of particular foibles, but of our most basic condition as parts of the natural world: our mortality, our particularity. Let me conclude with the rest of that passage.

Like the Victorian lady who refuses to look at her own nude body, some would like to create a world of less transitory stuff, reminding us only of our intellectual and social nature, never calling to mind our affinities with “lower” living creatures. The “denial of death,” to which psychiatrists call attention, reveals an attitude incompatible with the sort of self-acceptance which philosophers, from the ancients to Spinoza and on, have admired as a human excellence. My suggestion is not merely that experiencing nature causally promotes such self-acceptance, but also that those who fully accept themselves as part of the natural world lack the common drive to disassociate themselves from nature by replacing natural environments with artificial ones. A storm in the wilds helps us to appreciate our animal vulnerability, but, equally important, the reluctance to experience it may reflect an unwillingness to accept this aspect of ourselves. The person who is too ready to destroy the ancient redwoods may lack humility, not so much in the sense that he exaggerates his importance relative to others, but rather in the sense that he tries to avoid seeing himself as one among many natural creatures. (115)

Tom Hill thought that he was “one among many”—and thought that this was something anyone should be proud of. Rest in Peace, Tom. I’m grateful to have known you; I’m heartbroken by your death; and I wish you were still here for us to learn from.

Share

1

…the Deferential Wife is not servile if she tolerates an abusive husband because he is so ill that further strain would kill him, because protesting would deprive her of her only means of survival, or because she is collecting atrocity stories for her book against marriage. If there is fault in these situations, it seems inappropriate to call it servility. (96)

2

Here we arrive at one of the most important Kantian premises of Hill’s moral philosophy: that the ways in which humans are alike matter more than the ways in which we differ. You can see this especially clearly in Hill’s “Ideals of Human Excellence”:

Kant once wrote that he had been inclined to think that dignity and respect should vary with intellectual achievement and that therefore professors should be accorded the highest dignity, presumably vastly superior to that of common laborers. But, he says, Rousseau saved him from this error and taught him that the important ground of dignity is in every human being. Thus Kant seems to admit a temptation to what I call talent and/or achievement snobbery, but he found this to be incompatible with his idea of human dignity. (168)

item.title: There's still no excuse for giving bad talks
item.description: "Performing" isn't just entertainment.
item.content:encoded:
Thanks to everyone who shared or wrote me about my post on job talks. One of my inspirations was (of Small Potatoes fame), so it was a treat to see that he liked it.

The post also ended up on Daily Nous, where there’s been a bunch of commentary—including one grim, highly upvoted comment from a poster going by the name “Stop letting grad students waste their lives.”

Dr. Stop says no one should read career advice, because getting a job is 99% just a matter of having a fancy pedigree.

I have some thoughts on this.

Subscribe now

  1. My sympathy to Dr. Stop. It sucks being on the academic job market, and everybody hates being rejected by prospective employers.

  2. That said, if you’ve already left academia, why are you reading advice for PhD students?

  3. Also, the main advice here is catastrophically wrong. Your job talk doesn’t just matter 1%. It can easily sink an otherwise strong candidacy. This happens many times every year.

  4. Corollary: beware highly confident job talk advice from people who have neither given a job talk nor been on a hiring committee.

  5. Advisor quality matters, of course, but that’s no reason to ignore career advice. Great advisors are great in part because they give you career advice. That’s one of the main reasons why I posted my job talk advice in the first place—to level the playing field for students who didn’t hit the advisor jackpot. (See also on advisors as promoters.)

  6. The best point in here is that the reputation of your PhD program matters a lot—and not always for legitimate reasons. Even students with a strong CV and strong letters might struggle to get interviews if they’re coming from a program out of the “top 20.”

  7. Corollary: hiring committees owe it to the field not to overrate pedigree.

  8. Of course, I agree with the advice not to make yourself miserable. That’s why I said as much in my post. Read to the end before commenting!

  9. A lot of what you do in PhD programs is meant to get you a job—and kind of worthless otherwise. Not so for giving talks. Public speaking is an invaluable skill, and great talks are intrinsically good. They are a kind of achievement, which puts them among the best things in life. Of course, it’s nice if your talk is a smash hit that brings fame and fortune. But you can be proud of a good talk even if nobody else appreciates it.

  10. The single most important piece of advice I got while applying to graduate school was: “Don’t go for the sake of getting a job. Imagine you get hit by a bus right after defending your dissertation. Would you regret spending the last five or six years of your life on a PhD? If so, don’t do it.” This was fairly standard advice given to undergrads at UT Austin. It’s absolutely correct, even though in practice it’s hard not to get one’s hopes up once you’re on the PhD track.

There was also a follow-up from a certain satisfied palindrome:

I agree that intrinsic worth is good. But I couldn’t disagree more with the claim that contemporary philosophy is bad. Philosophy is great, actually! If you don’t believe me, read some Jake Nebel (formal ethics), Julia Staffel (epistemology), David Builes (metaphysics), Joe Heath (philosophy of social science), Agnes Callard (ancient), Laura Valentini (political), Lindsay Brainard (creativity & AI),, or Brian Hedden (ethics, etc.)—just to pick some authors off the top of my head.

Also, I have no idea what kind of “fundamental change to our entire economy” is supposed to benefit professional philosophers. More funding for universities would be nice, but that’s not “fundamental.” Maybe Mmhmm wants to bring back the philosopher-king?

Thankfully, there were other comments that I can more easily recommend. For example:

  • Louis deRosset says: don’t forget to “rehearse, rehearse, rehearse.”

  • Tom Hurka says:

    • “A crucial part of the job talk is the Q&A afterward: the audience want to know if you’re ‘in control of your material’…”

    • “I find the ‘this is the structure of the talk’ bit at the start of a job or other talk a waste of time. If I haven’t heard the talk yet, claims about what section 4 or 5 will be about mean little to me, and am I going to remember?”

  • UK Context adds: if there’s no teaching demonstration, people will use the job talk as evidence of a candidate’s teaching ability.

See also (make your talks “double-clickable”), Bryan Frances (look for non-academic talk advice), (brace for rejection), (most people should use one-page handouts), and Graduate Student (at some point you just have to use your best judgment).

Subscribe now

Share

Now I want to share a thought-provoking comment from Caligula’s Goat, which is about the idea of talks as “performances.”

I partially agree. Caligula’s Goat is right that we should prioritize substance above style—“dumplings over flowers,” as the saying goes.1 What ultimately matters in philosophy is the truth (understanding, wisdom, etc.). If we give jobs and accolades to those who merely cloak themselves in the trappings of truth, offering only truthy infotainment, we are going to do serious damage to the field over time and lose touch with our raison d’être.

That said, I don’t think a “good performance” is just a matter of entertainment value. When you go to the symphony, you want to be in touch with the deep stuff that composers are trying to get across. Nothing will kill that experience faster than a bad performance. If the performers are out of tune, out of sync, etc., the entire audience will be unable to get absorbed in the piece. The same is true for an academic talk. If the speaker is stumbling over words, losing their place, apologizing for being unprepared, running far over time, etc., it becomes that much harder for the audience to lock in and think about the underlying ideas.2

A good performance needn’t draw attention to itself. Often the best performances are the ones that do the opposite. Think about the rituals of classical music—the black-and-white dress, the performers’ silence between pieces—which tend to put the performers’ personalities in the background and keep the focus on the music.

That’s not to say that every musician should make the same choices about what goes in the background. Sometimes the clothes and makeup are supposed to stick out. See e.g. the alien outfits of Quebec’s Angine de Poitrine.

Emulating the rockstars of planet Earth, time-traveling explorers Klek and Khn de Poitrine marvel at hot dogs, pyramids, and rock in all its grandiosity. Their music acts like a vortex where dada rock, pythago-cubist mantras resonate.

So while I agree with Caligula’s Goat about the need to be substantial, I also agree with this reply from Not so fast:

Exactly. Academics need to be good at communication, both among ourselves and with the outside world. We can’t expect the public to trust us if we can’t even competently explain what we’re doing—ideally not just to each other!

A final story. Once, when I was preparing for a job talk, recommended taking lessons from an acting coach. This ended up being excellent advice. I liked doing the silly warm-ups and being forced to notice when I’m rushing, and it was refreshing to think about academic talks from the perspective of an actor. Yes, in a talk, the focus should be on the ideas. But until someone invents an idea ray capable of directly zapping our thoughts into the brains of others, we still have to resort to the ancient art of “saying words,” perhaps with the less ancient aid of “Powerpoint slides.” Since speaking is part of the process, we might as well try to do it properly.

So in closing: thank you, NYC-based actor and acting coach Stacey Linnartz, who I see is still taking new students. Next time I give a talk, I’ll do a silly warm-up in your honor.

“Dumplings over flowers” is one of my favorite Japanese proverbs (kotowaza)—up there with “Even monkeys fall from the tree” and “Failure is the mother of success.”

2

If a speaker has a stutter or other speech impediment, that’s different. Audiences know how to focus on the signal in such cases. It’s the obviously avoidable stumblings that are distracting.

item.title: I don't think Mamdani's grocery stores are going to work
item.description: The road to policy hell is paved with good intentions.
item.content:encoded:
At last, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled his plans for city-operated grocery stores in New York.

Today, I am proud to announce a collection of essential staples that will be predictably 30% cheaper at all five of our city-run grocery stores. This core set of goods will include all fresh produce, meat, and seafood, along with 20 other essential items like cheese, milk, and bread.

Here’s how it will work. Once a month, our five city-run grocery stores will set prices for this core set of goods at 30% below typical retail prices. No exceptions, no gimmicks. The savings will last for the entire month. That means no weekly fluctuations or sticker shock at the checkout line—not for our seniors living on fixed incomes, nor for the parents who rely on a regular supply of apple slices to keep toddler tantrums at bay.

In short, the city will use public funds to subsidize five stores to sell goods well below market prices. A small-scale endeavor. But will the effects be positive or negative?

Subscribe now

An obvious problem is that these stores will make life harder for existing bodegas and grocers. How can you stay in business if the city is using tax dollars to beat your prices? Mamdani’s solution is to limit his stores’ wares to a handful of staples—no alcohol, cigarettes, hot food, or scratch-offs.

We are not looking to compete with bodegas or grocery stores when it comes to their ability to survive. What we’re looking to do is to provide affordability that is guaranteed to New Yorkers.

But it doesn’t matter what the city is “looking” to do. What matters is the outcome, which is not hard to predict given basic economic principles. Any nearby stores that rely on selling staples to survive will die out, because they can’t possibly compete with a subsidized alternative that uses public funds to undercut their prices. It bears repeating: Mamdani’s stores are not just cutting their prices by being efficient or innovative. They are designed to systematically undercut the competition’s prices no matter how low they go, because the city’s prices are pegged to 70% of the prevailing market rate. There is no possible way for local stores to compete, no matter how well they operate or how sharply they cut their own profit rates, because every cut they make will cause the city to cut their prices even further (at taxpayer expense).1

This point was flatly ignored by some of Mamdani’s defenders. For example, Gustavo Gordillo, co-chair of the NYC DSA, had this to say:

If one publicly owned grocery store that brings prices down in the neighborhood is enough to put someone out of business — maybe they shouldn’t have been in that business in the first place.

This response would be reasonable if Mamdani’s stores were cutting prices by being efficient. In general, it’s good when bad firms get replaced with better ones. But that’s not how the program is designed. (If it were, there would be no need to peg the prices below market rate, and I wouldn’t be so pessimistic.) The program is designed to cut prices below any sustainable market rate by drawing on subsides from city hall. Mamdani’s stores will beat out local stores even if the local stores are more efficient. That means replacing good firms with bad ones. If this happens, more of New York’s resources will be spent operating grocery stores without any improvement for the average New Yorker.

In fact, New Yorkers will be stuck with another cost: lines. If a store is 30% cheaper than everywhere else (with comparable quality), people will flock to buy there. That means long, time-sucking lines.

Now, if Mamdani’s stores were run like normal grocery stores—i.e. without big subsidies—this problem would take care of itself. Mamdani could just open more stores, which would be profitable, and so the city would enjoy cheaper groceries and higher tax revenues. Life would admittedly be tough for the grocers who get outcompeted—but also, they’d be replaced by better stores, so on the whole the city would enjoy more prosperity. Lines would then shrink, because Mamdani stores would be more plentiful. Win-win-win.

But, by design, Mamdani’s program can’t work like this. Thanks to subsidies from the city, Mamdani’s stores can afford to be less efficient, so opening more of them would likely make the city less prosperous. The more Mamdani stores there are, the worse the overall economy of the city. That means no easy solution to the problem of lines.2

(Well, there is one booby prize. If the lines are bad enough, local grocers will still be able to compete for customers—but that’s just to say that the lower prices may not be worth the wait.)

Share

The fundamental problem with Mamdani’s grocery stores is that they are profoundly negative sum. They are destroying economic value (through deadweight loss and misallocation) in order to redistribute a chunk of what remains to those lucky few who live on the right block and shop at the right time of day.

That said, there are real benefits to progressive redistribution, which shouldn’t be gainsaid. The poor gain more from an extra dollar than the rich gain from two extra dollars. But that’s no defense of Mamdani’s stores, since they aren’t even well-designed for redistribution. Notice that anyone can shop there—there is no means testing. By contrast, food stamps are designed to help the poor, and they don’t cause long lines or put more efficient grocers out of business.

Let me also emphasize that none of my arguments rely on conservative, libertarian, or centrist moral principles. I’m just doing basic policy analysis based on boring, well-understood principles of economics—nothing up my sleeves.

My point is that the (legitimate) leftist aim of helping poor people get affordable groceries is not best achieved by plowing tax dollars into high-cost public grocers. There are other means to the same end that wouldn’t face the same problems: food stamps, a basic income, subsidies for competitive grocers—even certain kinds of state-owned enterprises, viz. those that have to compete fairly with the private sector (rather than being allowed to operate at a loss thanks to taxpayer subsidies).

I might be wrong. Maybe Mamdani’s managers will be public-spirited types who outcompete the private alternatives despite lacking an economic incentive to do so. It’s certainly conceivable. But given what we know about economics and psychology, it ain’t likely. Consider this post my confident prediction, to be revisited in a year or two.

Subscribe now

My takeway from Grocery-gate is that the US desperately needs better policy analysis. In general, we are suffering from a degradation of the means being proposed to our political ends. (See also: Trump’s tariffs.)

Mamdani, of course, is not the first person to squander their good intentions of feeding the hungry on policies that do anything but. Let me conclude with a tragedy on a much larger scale: the story of Ethiopia’s famine of the 1980s, as recounted by Stanford’s Leif Wenar.

Ethiopia received significant food aid each year during the decade after the famine of the mid-1980’s, normally equivalent to about 10% of its total food production. During this period, and despite the fact that there was enough food in-country to meet the nutritional needs of all Ethiopians, almost half of Ethiopian households remained food-insecure. A significant amount of food was distributed through food relief projects, yet relatively little of this food reached those in need. Well-off districts were just as likely to receive the imported food as very poor districts, and on average less than 23% of food-insecure households received any food. Moreover, much of the food that was distributed to food-secure households ended up being resold on local markets, depressing food prices and diminishing incentives for domestic production, thus increasing food insecurity and stimulating another campaign for food aid the next year.

Those who donated food to Ethiopia probably had good intentions. They were looking to help. But the actual effects of dumping food into the country were disastrous. The benefits were temporary and ineptly distributed; the shortage of food itself was ultimately exacerbated. The do-gooders’ fatal mistake, as Wenar sees it, was their incuriosity about the way local institutions actually function.

Ironically, this objection is one that we’re used to seeing from the left against effective altruists. When it comes to groceries, the Mamdani left should take its own advice. Instead of running gimmicky stores that waste money, give poor people food stamps or tax refunds.3

1

It’s worth mentioning that grocery stores don’t have anything remotely near 30% profit margins. Aswath Damodaran at NYU Stern puts US retail (grocery and food) as having net margins of 1.32% last year. The grocers themselves say their margin is 2.1%. In fact, even gross margins can be below 30%, which means Mamdani’s stores may end up selling their food for less than the price at which they bought it!

One more thing. Don’t expect Mamdani’s stores to pop up in so-called “food deserts” bereft of private grocers; these have turned out to be overhyped. The New Yorker got it right: “there is little evidence to support the idea that bringing supermarkets to neighborhoods that lack them has a measurable effect on what residents eat.”

2

The stores could avoid lines by running a lottery to choose who gets to shop there each month—but this would destroy the predictability that Mamdani is promising.

3

For a highly informative response to some of Wenar’s critiques of EA, see this post from .

item.title: The efficiency vs. equity dilemma is (usually) fake
item.description: Congestion pricing, algorithmic bias, price gouging—the world is full of false policy dilemmas. The only way out is up, using Thomas Schelling's 2d analysis.
item.content:encoded:
A while back, New York City was debating the merits of congestion pricing, which charges drivers a fee to enter high-traffic areas, and the city found itself facing a classic dilemma of efficiency versus equity.

Congestion pricing is efficient: if you don’t charge downtown drivers, you’re letting them freely impose various costs on others—pollution, noise, traffic, and so on. These costs can be enormous. In a 2025 working paper, Enrico Moretti and Harrison Wheeler estimate the cost of nationwide traffic noise at $110 billion—with a “b”! Charging a fee forces drivers to “internalize” such costs, which encourages those drivers who have a good alternative to take it, while allowing those who really need to drive to do so.

But as critics pointed out, congestion pricing is also inequitable: if we charge every driver a flat fee, poor drivers will be hit much harder. Egalitarians don’t like the idea of charging the same $9 toll to a communter on their way to make minimum wage as to a billionaire joyriding in their Rolls-Royce.

What should we do? Should we prioritize efficiency—or prioritize equity?

Trick question: you don’t have to choose. In the ethics of policy, the efficiency/equity dilemma typically arises as a sort of mirage, which disappears once we properly lay out the space of all policy options at our disposal. To do this, we need to use what Thomas Schelling called “two-dimensional” policy analysis.

But first, lest you think I’m just talking about cars in NY, I want to show you more examples. Once you know how to spot the efficiency/equity dilemma, you’ll notice it’s everywhere.

Subscribe now

1. Biased algorithms

Consider the case of algorithmic bias. In the US, many judges base their sentencing and detention decisions on estimates from algorithms like Equivant’s COMPAS, which assigns a defendant a risk score based on their age, history, education, and so on.

This at least could be efficient: if the algorithm really does give high-quality estimates (a big “if”), the system will generate more public safety, on average, per year of incarceration.

But even if efficient, such algorithms are arguably inequitable. Case in point, a hugely influential 2016 report from ProPublica accused COMPAS of being “biased against blacks,” because the algorithm’s errors followed a troubling pattern:

  • “The formula was particularly likely to falsely flag black defendants as future criminals, wrongly labeling them this way at almost twice the rate as white defendants.”

  • “White defendants were mislabeled as low risk more often than black defendants.”

To be clear, ProPublica wasn’t alleging that COMPAS was designed to discriminate against black defendants, or that the algorithm explicitly took account of race. Rather, the problem was that the algorithm seems to have violated certain statistical criteria of fairness by tending to make errors in favor of one group and to the detriment of another.1 So there’s a dilemma: either we have biased decisions or benighted ones.

2. Price gouging

Some states in the US ban “price gouging,” which they define as raising prices on certain goods in an emergency.

Now, Econ 101 tells us that so-called “price gouging” will generally be efficient. If the price of toilet paper can go up, so can the quantity supplied; you avoid the problem of shortages. But you also create a problem of inequity: the rich will have an easier time paying $10 a roll (or whatever the price may be).

For a real example, consider Mike Munger’s story of the Goldsboro yahoos. When Hurricane Fran hit North Carolina in 1996, Raleigh lost power, and people there lost access to ice and cooling. “Insulin, baby formula, and other necessities immediately became susceptible to spoilage in the 92+ degree heat.” Some enterprising “yahoos” drove in from four hours away in Goldsboro, using chainsaws to clear the path for their two rented freezer trucks, which they’d stuffed with 500 bags of ice. The yahoos set up shop; Munger says they were selling at over $8 a bag (having bought at $1.70). People were, evidently, more than willing to wait in line to buy ice at that price. Thus the yahoos were more efficiently distributing the state’s ice, which was no longer languishing in Goldsboro while insulin spoiled in Raleigh. But the customers still resented the inequity. Eventually, someone must have called the cops, who arrested the yahoos, impounded the trucks—and all the while, the ice went undistributed.

Munger’s outrage leaps off the page:

And now we are back to where I started: the citizens, the prospective buyers being denied a chance to buy ice… they clapped. Clapped, cheered, and hooted, as the vicious ice sellers were handcuffed and arrested. Some of those buyers had been standing in line for five minutes or more, and had been ready to pay 4 times as much as the maximum price the state would allow. And they clapped as the police, at gunpoint, took that opportunity away from them.

And yet—to the chagrin of Munger and many other pro-marketeers—it doesn’t really matter how many times you preach the gospel of Econ 101. People just really do think price-gouging is immoral! If that’s right, then the dilemma is real: either we have to live with shortages or else let the poor get iced out.

3. Zoning and rent control

Say there’s a lot of unmet demand for rental housing in a nice neighborhood. It seems efficient to let developers build housing there—the developers get big bucks, and the renters get better housing. But if the rents are high, the poor will be priced out: another inequity.

One solution to the inequity is “inclusionary zoning”: require developers to set aside a certain percentage of new housing at below-market rates. But this makes it less profitable to build housing, which directly creates inefficiencies: there will be some developments that never happen, despite the presence of many willing renters, because the costs of inclusionary zoning make the prospect a financial loser for the developer. Again, the dilemma is a painful one. Either efficiency at the poor’s expense, or poverty-relief that gunks up the system.

Much the same point arises with rent control. If you let landlords raise rents, that will tend to increase the quantity (and quality!) of the housing supply in an efficient way. But it can seem inequitable. When a neighborhood becomes desirable, poor tenants may be unable to pay their rising rents, and so they are displaced by rich newcomers.

In defense of efficiency

I could add a zillion more examples.2 But you get the idea. Often the economically efficient policy is inequitable, and the equitable policy is inefficient.

You might respond by saying: so much for efficiency! We are human beings, with human rights, and we shouldn’t be violating one another’s dignity for the sake of some inhuman, technocratic value of “efficiency.”

But this response is less attractive than it sounds at first. The reason why is that, in the context of economic policy debates, “efficiency” doesn’t refer to some bloodless bureaucratic metric. It just refers to people getting what they want and need.

More specifically, “efficient” often just means Pareto-optimal, which is a fancy way to say “no win-wins left on the table.” So, when the Goldsboro yahoos are banned from selling ice to willing customers, that’s inefficient, because there was a win-win left on the table: money for the yahoos, ice for the good people of Raleigh. Infamously, this notion of efficiency is consistent with as much inequity as you like. (Notice that every outcome of a zero-sum game is “efficient,” including “I get everything, you get nothing.”) But that’s just to say that efficiency isn’t all that we want. We should still be loath to live with inefficiencies—unless we’re against win-wins, in which case we’ve got other problems.

“Escaping the dilemma”

Usually, I like to beat people over the head with the reality of tradeoffs and the unsolvability of the big problems with the human condition. But in this case, our problems might actually be solvable, thanks to an idea from the economist (and hero of the blog) Thomas Schelling, in a strange yet wonderful article called “Economic Reasoning and the Ethics of Policy.”

The article is strange because it rambles. Schelling talks about winning arguments with his students over gas rationing; he dwells on the unusual example of runway lights at airports. The article is also ethically a bit tone-deaf compared to Schelling’s other papers, a point stressed by the philosopher Bernard Williams (in a jewel of a review).3

I cite these reasons not to disparage Schelling’s paper, but to explain why its core insight has been so criminally overlooked.4

Schelling’s insight is that the efficiency/equity dilemma arises when we try to solve two problems using one policy. The solution is to solve the two problems using two policies. Kill two birds with two stones.

For example, in the case of congestion pricing, we have two problems: we want to charge drivers to minimize externalities, and we want to ease burdens on the poor. If we are thinking in one policy dimension, we are stuck with a tradeoff. The more we charge, the more pain for the poor. The less we charge, the more pollution, noise, and traffic. But why assume the solution has to lie along that one dimension, i.e. how much to charge drivers? We could instead think in two dimensions. We adjust congestion pricing to whatever point best addresses pollution (etc.), and then we separately address the problem of poverty using a dedicated anti-poverty policy. One option is to make the policy a kind of local or targeted thing—think: vouchers for poor drivers. Another option is simply to be more generous at a big-picture level, e.g. by making the tax code more progressive. Either way, it’s possible to achieve a win-win on efficiency and equity compared to any of the original policy options we had in the 1d space we started from.

The solution is perfectly general. Typically, our dilemma arises when there are two problems, such as a supply problem and a poverty problem. And we’re usually better off solving the two problems in two policy dimensions. For example, in an emergency, we might allow prices to rise while offering cash relief to the poor. In the case of algorithmic bias, we might use the most accurate algorithms while using other policies to address racial inequities directly. Rather than rent control, we might prefer uncapped rents and vouchers for poor tenants (the US has something like this, called “Section 8 housing,” which deserves a lot more credit than it gets).

That said, there’s a reason why we don’t live in a magic high-dimensional world where all our policy dreams come true. Often there are deep political or institutional obstacles facing the two-dimensional solution. As Schelling explains it, this is the crucial limitation of “the two-dimensional approach.”

Most important, the reasoning does not demonstrate that the superior policy or program technique is actually achievable. In particular it may depend on institutions that do not exist, or politics that are unacceptable, or administrative determinations that are infeasible.

But this is, notably, a very different problem from the original efficiency/equity dilemma. We have transformed a policy problem into a political problem. That is often enough to allow for significant progress. The political problem might be just as insoluble—but then it again, it might not.

Even better: sometimes going 2d will make your solution more politically tractable. One important example of this arises in tax policy. We seem to face a dilemma: equity favors a progressive tax system, but sometimes the most progressive taxes are painfully inefficient (e.g. wealth taxes), and usually the rich and powerful will fight them tooth and nail. Again, we have two distinct problems—equity and efficiency—that we are trying to solve by adjusting only one dimension: the progressiveness of the tax code. But Yale’s Ian Shapiro reminds us that we have a second dimension to consider—the progressiveness of government spending.

I think the trouble with the politics of tax is people tend to not think about the taxing side and the spending side together. So, you know, people jump up and down that we should have more progressive taxation. Well, progressive taxation is often a very costly way to raise taxes. And the cheapest ways to raise taxes are actually the more regressive ways, like a VAT, which is pretty regressive. But if you have progressivity on the spending side, it doesn’t really matter if it’s regressive on the taxing side.

So I’ve argued that the best way to tax is just to raise taxes in the most efficient way possible and then worry about the distributive dimensions on the spending side. Especially in a country like this, where exit costs are very low for billionaires.

The next time you’re feeling stuck in a policy dilemma, consider how many distinct problems you’re trying to solve—and how many distinct policies you’re using to solve them. Sometimes there is no need to suffer in n dimensions. There’s a solution waiting for you in dimension n + 1.
