4

Another problem, also serious, is that bureaucracies may mistreat and misunderstand minorities. See e.g. ’s (2023) “The Challenge of Policing Minorities in a Liberal Society.”

5

Unless you’re willing to do away with the division of labor and go back into a pre-industrial society—which, you know, I get it, but you’re probably going to miss modern medicine, video games, restaurants, and AC.

6

Seriously! I haven’t argued that capitalism is optimal or even acceptable. I’ve just argued that some of the arguments purporting to show that ethics is impossible under capitalism would equally show that ethics is impossible under socialism, too.

As I’ve put it elsewhere, some problems are “trans-systemic.”

item.title: Down iff Under
item.description: That’s not a listicle...THIS is a listicle
item.content:encoded:
Last month, I moved back to Australia to take a dream job at the Australian National University, where I’d been a visitor for nearly a decade. My (Aussie) wife and I dearly miss our friends and family in the US—and I will forever love UNC—but we’re grateful to have found permanent jobs in the same city at last, and we’re delighted to be back Down Under.

In hono(u)r of Australia, I thought I’d share five of my favo(u)rite facts about this remarkable country.

Share

1. Australia is larger than the Moon with respect to diameter

Now this is wild. If you walk west-to-east across the widest part of Australia, you’ll end up walking roughly 4,000 kilometers (~2,500 miles). The Moon’s diameter, meanwhile, is just under 3,500 kilometers.

Wow!

Here’s a neat visualization:

We think of the Moon as being this gigantic hunk of rock, unbelievably far away—clearly, our intuitions are out of whack. Either the Moon is way closer than we think, or way smaller than we realize.

Another way to wrap your head around this is to think about what Australia would look like in the sky.

For reference, the Moon looks like this:

A celestial Australia, at a comparable distance, would look like this:

Neat, huh?

Now let’s move on to the next Australia fact.

Subscribe now

2. Australia is larger than the Moon with respect to population

This is crazy. The Moon has been around for roughly 4.5 billion years. Australia became a separate continent only 50 million years ago. The indigenous peoples of Australia have lived here 65,000 years, and the federation of Australia wasn’t here until a mere 125 years ago.

And yet, Australia’s population absolutely dwarfs that of the Moon, by a margin of 28 million.

What’s going on? Part of the problem is that the Moon has limited options for work, recreation, and nightlife. They have essentially no offerings of gourmet coffee or authentic Italian food, two of the classic draws of Melbourne’s laneways. They are also one of the few holdouts where bubble tea has yet to become available. Indeed, the surface features of the Moon have barely changed in 3 billion years, owing partly to a lack of plate tectonics.

That’s not all. The Moon’s mass is so puny (1.2% of the Earth’s) that there’s not enough gravity to sustain a robust atmosphere. Rather than having a five-layer atmosphere like ours, the Moon has only a single thin exosphere, composed overwhelmingly of helium, neon, and argon. This makes it difficult to breathe on the Moon, and it also means that regolith on the surface isn’t subject to erosion by wind (or water, for that matter), leaving it spiky and dangerous to inhale.

Moving on:

3. Australia is larger than the Moon with respect to gross sales of indie video games

This is completely insane.

Australian indie developers have put out some of the most beloved and original video games of the last decade. In 2017, the Adelaide-based Team Cherry released Hollow Knight, a brutally difficult metroidvania that went on to sell over 15 million copies. Last year’s sequel, Hollow Knight: Silksong, has already sold over 7 million copies. (No, I haven’t beaten it on Steel Soul.)1

The quirky breakout of 2019 was Untitled Goose Game, in which you play as a mischievous goose terrorizing a village for obscure purposes. That sold over a million copies. Credit to House House, based in Melbourne.

And who could forget Cult of the Lamb, the cutesy ovine roguelike in which you play as a satanic cult-leader? Massive Monster, also Melbourne-based, released this one in 2022, and it’s sold over 7 million copies.

The Moon, by contrast, has sold precisely zero copies of its indie video games in the years since 2017.

Pathetic.

4. Australia is more ethnically diverse than the Moon

In the middle of the 20th century, still the era of the baleful “White Australia” policy, Australia was far more ethnically homogeneous than it is today. 98% of the population was white in 1947; roughly 1% was indigenous Australian, with an Asian population of only 0.2% or so.2

After WWII, a series of changes led to a more ethnically diverse population. First the country began welcoming non-British Europeans (such as the Italians who brought their espresso machines to Lygon St in Melbourne). Then, from 1958 to 1975, the country passed a series of acts dismantling the the Immigration Restriction Act (1901)—the legal cornerstone of the White Australia policy—and replacing it with laws against racial discrimination.

The result has been a steady stream of immigrants contributing to the vibrancy of Australian culture. The country is still majority European in ancestry—and within that, mostly Anglo-Celtic—but now 17% of the country is of Asian descent, 3% Middle Eastern or North African, and 3% indigenous to Australia. (Most indigenous Australians are Aboriginal Australians from the mainland; around 8% are Torres Strait Islanders, an ethnically distinct group originating from the islands north of Queensland.)

By contrast, the Moon has no ethnic diversity to speak of. Nor is there any evidence of an indigenous population, human or otherwise. Also striking is the demography of the Moon’s tourists: all 12 of the people who have ever walked on the Moon’s surface have been White American males. Until recently, only White American males had so much as flown to the Moon; that streak wasn’t broken until last April, when NASA’s Artemis II mission featured a four-person crew that was neither all-white, all-male, nor all-American.

Finally:

5. Australia has overtaken the Moon with respect to philosophy Substack metrics

Last week, my humble Substack hit a milestone:

That is small potatoes compared to (611k), (155k), or (51k). But 3k is still more subscribers than all lunar Substackers combined.

It is also, to be honest, way more than I ever needed or expected. As a token of my thanks, here’s my favorite Australian animal:

See you next week—

This sentence is false & you won’t subscribe to Big iff True

PS

My wife wanted me to add that Australians made vital contributions to the invention of wifi and cochlear implants.

She was less proud of this other Aussie original:

1

But I have beaten every boss in the Hall of Gods on Radiant.

2

In the first seven Australian censuses, the population of Aboriginal Australians (“full bloods”) was not included in the total population count. This omission, far from a fluke, was mandated by section 127 of the constitution:

In reckoning the numbers of the people of the Commonwealth, or of a State or other part of the Commonwealth, aboriginal natives should not be counted.

This part of the constitution was struck down in a referendum in 1967. (I am reminded of the notoriously racist “three-fifths compromise” in my home country’s constitution.)

One sometimes hears—even from sitting politicians—that Aboriginal Australians were excluded from the census because of a “flora and fauna act.” This is a curious myth: there was never an act with such a name, nor do the terms “flora” and “fauna” appear in the constitution, nor was there ever legislation referring to Aboriginal Australians in such terms.

item.title: It is what it is
item.description: What’s big is big. What’s true is true.
item.content:encoded:
A man’s gotta do what a man’s gotta do.

Boys will be boys.

I am what I am.

You do you.

Kids will be kids.

A baby’s gotta do what a baby’s gotta do.

Communication is not unique to humans, but human communication is unique. Other primates can be taught to say no as a refusal. Only humans say no as negation. “No man is an island,” “Big kids don’t cry,” “There is nothing I would not do for those who are really my friends.” These are categorically more sophisticated than “No” in response to “Want a banana?” We stack symbols upon symbols to create expressions of arbitrary complexity and infinite unfurling novelty. Some of our capabilities we understand at once. Others we must discern through guesswork and experiment, studying our minds as we might the principles of mechanics or electromagnetism, or as a North American might speculate about the rules of cricket from the stands. Nobody taught you the order of adjectives. But they do come in order: “cute little tan Australian mammal” is correct, “Canadian brown big amazing bear” is not. When did you learn this? How did you learn this?

No means no.

Yes means yes.

Rules are rules.

Orders are orders

My name is my name.

Your business is your business.

The central purpose of communication is to present and absorb information. The essence of information is awareness of what is the case. How to get beyond such platitudes? We build a model. We think of a conversation as characterized by a state of current information—the common ground—understood as a set of ways the world could be, or a set of possible worlds. By default, anything is possible. The set is very big. Assertions add information, which is to say that they narrow down the set of possible worlds in the common ground. If we assert that the boss is clueless, we remove from consideration those possible worlds where the boss is savvy; such worlds are, for us, no longer live possibilities. (Notice: it takes more information to end up with fewer possible worlds, just as it takes more force to squish a foam ball to a smaller size.) In this model, information means something very specific. A piece of information is itself a set of possible worlds—intuitively, the set of worlds consistent with the information. To share the information that My name is “Daniel” is to throw out all possibilities where my name is anything else.

What’s done is done.

What’s past is past.

It is what it is.

A = A.

Qué será, será.

Whatever will be, will be.

It’s a powerful framework: to communicate is, fundamentally, the joint activity of ruling out possible worlds. But isn’t something missing? Suppose I say my name is “Daniel.” You may well learn the truth of what I say. But you also learn a further fact, which is not said—namely, that I said it, in this context, knowing all that I know. This basic observation could not be more important. That something is said is often more informative than what is said. H. P. Grice’s legendary example: a philosophy professor, writing a letter of recommendation, says only “Mr. X’s command of English is excellent, and his attendance at tutorials has been regular. Yours, etc.” The writer doesn’t have to come out and say what he thinks of Mr. X’s abilities; from the fact that the subject was avoided, the reader can infer there was nothing nice to say. Grice called such inferences conversational implicature, and thought of them as flowing from the combination of what is said in conversation and what we know about conversation—specifically, that parties to a conversation obey a “Cooperative Principle.” We assume people are not withholding relevant information, making baseless assertions, and going on pointless tangents. Since this assumption is common knowledge, we can exploit it to convey information far beyond what we say explicitly.

Our talk exchanges do not normally consist of a succession of disconnected remarks, and would not be rational if they did. They are characteristically, to some degree at least, cooperative efforts…

—H. P. Grice, “Logic and Conversation”

Business is business.

A fact’s a fact.

Dienst ist Dienst und Schnaps ist Schnaps.1

A deal’s a deal.

A win is a win.

それはそれ、これはこれ。2

Could even this be too simple? Our sentences have meanings (“semantics”); we use the Cooperative Principle to convey messages beyond these meanings (“pragmatics”). But doesn’t this still seem to imply that what is conveyed depends only on meaning and context? And yet two sentences with the same “meaning”—the same set of possible worlds—could implicate different messages, even in one and the same context. A boy has shoved a girl in the mud. The girl’s parent complains to the teacher. The teacher might say, “Boys will be boys,” or “It is what it is,” or “Rules are rules.” These implicate very different things, and yet, in a clear sense, they mean the same thing. In each case, the information carried by the sentence is zero, in the sense that no possible worlds are ruled out. (In what possible world could rules fail to be rules?) Not all semantically equivalent statements are equal. One wants to say, not all tautologies are tautologies.

An engagement is an engagement.

Work is work.

Fair’s fair.

Power is power.

A rose is a rose is a rose is a rose.

Is it the model’s fault? Should we give up on possible worlds, common ground, and all the rest? Let’s not be hasty. Maybe the model is doing what it’s supposed to do. It reveals a fundamental dynamic. It tells us something deep and true about part of language—and therefore something at least partly true of language as a whole. As we use sentences to convey more than their meanings, could we use a model to study more than its content? The model makes things tractable, simple, amenable to calculation and explicit deduction. Language is often nothing like this. But for that reason we cannot explicitly represent it to ourselves as it is in reality. We must view it through a pinhole, in miniature, or in schematic form. But a thing is not its image. The map is not the territory. Nor should it have to be.

And that’s that.

Subscribe to subscribe

1

“Duty is duty, and leisure is leisure.”

2

Sore wa sore, kore wa kore — “that is that, and this is this.”

item.title: Moral rights without metaphysical baggage
item.description: Against the edgy metaphysical argument for collectivism, ft. Thomson on bees.
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve ever chatted with postliberals, you’ve probably heard a lot of scoffing at individual rights, such as the right not to have one’s property destroyed. There are, to be sure, many legitimate complaints one could have about contemporary rights discourse:

  • Rights claims are often vague, saying little about who should enforce them and how.

  • It’s not obvious how we could have natural rights, independent of politics, culture, and religion. (Even John Locke begins his chapter on property with the premise that God gave us the world in common.)

  • Merely calling something a “right” is often unpersuasive, since people typically disagree about who has which rights.

  • People love making frivolous rights claims. For example, when some Celebes crested macaques used a photographer’s camera to take selfies, PETA argued (in court, repeatedly) that the monkeys should be given copyright.

But today I want to talk about my least favorite objection to rights—viz., that individual rights presuppose an individualist conception of human nature. To say that people have rights, the objection goes, is to imply that we are self-contained atoms, fundamentally dependent on nobody outside of ourselves. It may even imply that we are purely self-interested, or that we reject any deep group identity (race, ethnicity, family, nationality, religion, etc.). On this view, rights are a concession to our egoistic and competitive nature, designed to insulate us from our communities and their pesky expectations. For this reason, rights can seem antithetical to any social reform that would restructure social relations to be more cooperative and egalitarian. No wonder rights strike so many progressives as reactionary propaganda. The moment someone proposes a cooperative scheme, e.g. government-provided healthcare, people start invoking their rights to justify not contributing. And no wonder the postliberal right sees individual rights as an annoying hindrance. The moment someone tries to use the state to enforce traditional norms, e.g. male-led households, dissidents cite their rights to insist on their nontraditional lifestyles.

Naturally, I often disagree with the postliberals’ conclusions. People should get to choose their own lifestyles, and they should have some veto power when the community comes along demanding use of their body and property. These are generalizations, of course, not absolute principles. (I love my Aussie Medicare.) But any decent society should aspire, where possible, to give its members the freedom to shape their own lives. Such freedom is made possible by individual rights.

The question is: where does the objection to rights go wrong?

Subscribe now

Atom and ego

The objection is really an argument with two premises:

  1. We can’t have individual rights unless we’re egoistic atoms.

  2. We’re not egoistic atoms.

So: we can’t have individual rights.

Since the argument is logically valid, the only way out is to reject a premise. But which? Should we defend the picture of humans as egoistic atoms? Or should we try to develop a theory of rights without such metaphysical baggage?

Personally, I’d rather give up the baggage. It’s just not true that people are purely selfish and self-sufficient.

For one thing, it is just indisputable that human beings have inherently social desires. We desire status. We desire affection. We desire to belong, and we desire what is best for the groups we belong to. We desire to be remembered by and to contribute to future generations, as Sam Scheffler argues in Death & the Afterlife. When Thomas Hobbes portrays humans as self-interested machines in Leviathan, he is missing something about the kinds of beings we are.1

Also important is that we are profoundly interdependent. Because we evolved to have big brains, we can’t fully develop in utero, on pain of making childbirth even more of an ordeal for mothers than it already is. That’s why newborn giraffes are basically ready to rock (though it takes them a few tries to stand up), whereas newborn humans are whiny, burpy messes that take years to develop any useful capabilities, such as writing posts on Substack.

Share

Babies are therefore dependent on caregivers—as are the sick and very elderly. But even the healthiest adults are kidding themselves if they think they’re truly self-sufficient. I’m writing this on a laptop running software I don’t understand, built from components I don’t know how to make, made of materials I don’t know how to acquire, on a contintent I could never have reached on my own. The mere fact that I bought this laptop online, using written language and fiat currency, is a triple miracle of cooperation.

With help from others, I can do all kinds of amazing things (like flying to Australia). Left to my own devices, I would maybe survive another month or two, but I’d be miserable and vulnerable. My standard of living would collapse in an instant.

The idea that we are self-contained individuals—able and content to exist alone—is not even close to true.

Subscribe now

Rights as social technology

But if we’re not metaphysical loners, how could we have individual rights?

The answer is that your rights don’t just flow from your own nature. Rather than being the product of an individual essence, rights are better understood as solutions to problems of collective action.

Suppose we live in a band of hunter-gatherers. We’d have a much easier time hunting and gathering if we had tools—and, thankfully, we know how to make and maintain them. But doing so is laborious. We need an incentive to do such labor. One solution is to give ownership rights to whoever makes a tool. A right is, in essence, the private ability to invoke communal norms. If I steal the spear you just spent all day making, you can say, “That’s mine,” and if I shrug you off, you can expect the community to have your back in the ensuing dispute. Thus your rights protect you from being expropriated, which encourages you to invest in the stuff you need.

That’s not all. Rights can also allow you to benefit from helping others, via private transfers. Suppose you’ve got enough spears, but your bandmates don’t. If you make extra, you can exchange them for other things of value. (Not that you’re required to do so; you could just give me a spear as a gift, if you like me.) This feature of rights makes them flexible: they let you use the power of the community to determine, on the spot, what will happen to certain resources.

Individual rights thus let people internalize the benefits of their own productive labor. That is a powerful solution to problems of expropriation and underproduction.

To be clear, I’m not suggesting that rights are the only way to solve collective action problems, or that they’re always the best way. We could imagine a band that collectively organizes the production and distribution of spears—if anyone slacks off (or tampers with the distribution), they get punished. This particular venture may be more trouble than it’s worth. But in many cases, collective organization turns out to be more effective than private ownership, as shown by decades of empirical research. Elinor Ostrom points out that some resources are difficult to carve up into individual-sized pieces (such as highly heterogenous farmland), and that private ownership does worse in situations where the goods in question can’t be privately improved very much (e.g. the rocky mountainsides of Switzerland, where communal farms have persisted since the Middle Ages). Finally, some goods—viz. “nonexcludable” goods like national security and clean air—are difficult to make private, since the owners can’t easily decide who gets to enjoy them.

Now, at this point, you might well be wondering why I am resting so much on a thought experiment. Sure, it’s one thing to imagine that hunter-gatherers might benefit from a system of private property rights. But didn’t we learn from Marx and Engels that private property was an innovation of capitalism, and thus a fairly recent development in human history?

In a word: no. As the anthropologist Manvir Singh has argued, every human society has some form of private property, including foragers and hunter-gatherers.

All hunter-gatherers had private property, even the Aché [of Paraguay]. Individual Aché owned bows, arrows, axes and cooking implements. Women owned the fruit they collected. Even meat became private property as it was handed out. Hill explained: ‘If I set my armadillo leg on [a fern leaf] and went out for a minute to take a pee in the forest and came back and somebody took it? Yeah, that was stealing.’

Some proponents of primitive communism concede that foragers owned small trinkets but insist they didn’t own wild resources. But this too is mistaken. Shoshone families owned eagle nests. Bearlake Athabaskans owned beaver dens and fishing sites. Especially common is the ownership of trees. When an Andaman Islander man stumbled upon a tree suitable for making canoes, he told his group mates about it. From then, it was his and his alone. Similar rules existed among the Deg Hit’an of Alaska, the Northern Paiute of the Great Basin, and the Enlhet of the arid Paraguayan plains. In fact, by one economist ’s estimate, more than 70 per cent of hunter-gatherer societies recognised private ownership over land or trees.

Other foragers [besides the Mbuti] punished stealing, too. The Ute of Colorado whipped thieves. The Ainu of Japan sliced their earlobes off. For the Yaghan of Tierra del Fuego, accusing someone of robbery was a ‘deadly insult’. Lorna Marshall, who spent years living with the Kalahari !Kung, reported that a man was once killed for taking honey. Through violence towards offenders, foragers reified private property.

Again, I want to emphasize the limited role of private property in these societies, which are also governed by communal rules that don’t look anything like individual rights. Rules of etiquette, for example, often just say what everyone’s supposed to do, rather than giving anyone the discretion to decide what shall be done.

Let’s zoom out for a moment and put this in perspective. A society has to decide what will happen with its resources. We could leave people to their own devices—in which case, we should expect lots of squabbling and not much cooperation. Or we could try to impose a system for deciding on the use of resources, backed by the threat of social sanction. Our system might be centralized, in which case we agree to follow top-down commands or rules. Or the system might be decentralized, in which case individuals are given some local spheres of authority at ground level. Rights are the mechanism of a decentralized system. They allow a society to make systematic decisions in a bottom-up way.

So far I have been focused on property rights, and while I think there’s a case to be made that any society (even a realistic socialist utopia) would be better off with some kinds of private property, the case is just overwhelming that any decent society should accord people rights over their own bodies.

Think about the following grotesque wrongs:

  • Infecting people without consent to study the effects of a disease

  • Involuntary sterilizations

  • Forced early-term abortions

  • Sexual assault

  • The publication of “revenge porn”

Harming, changing, or revealing someone’s body is profoundly wrong if done without consent. The fact that individual consent matters is a telltale sign that we are in the realm of rights. In this case, the point of body rights is to allow each person to use the power of the collective to enforce decisions about what will happen to their own body. If someone is trying to force themselves on you, your rights are a way to empower you to call upon others—whether to protect yourself, punish the violator, or seek reparations.2

This particular conception of the individual’s bodily autonomy is, to my mind, very hard to beat. Anyone who conceives of bodily rights as mere “ideology” is in danger of self-radicalizing to the point of silliness.3

Conclusion

There is, I admit, a kernel of truth in the idea that rights presuppose a conception of the individual. There would be little need for rights in a world where everybody shares the same interests. If we all want what’s best for everyone, then you don’t have to worry about being expropriated by me: I won’t take your spear unless I need it more—in which case, you’ll want me to take it. A natural harmony between everybody’s interests would therefore make it unnecessary for society to organize cooperation, either through central planning, or through devolved decision-making (i.e. rights).

But while I think there is some truth to this point, I don’t think it’s a threat to rights.

Even if people’s interests do align, that doesn’t mean we’ll all agree about what should be done. Not everyone will believe that our interests are all perfectly in harmony, and we will still have to deal with deep disagreements about the likely effects of various actions, such as the use of vaccines, the raising of interest rates, and the construction of data centers. Good old factual uncertainty, even on its own, has a way of fracturing unanimity of preference.

But the deeper point is that people do have conflicting interests. Earlier I mentioned one potential source of conflict: inherently social desires, like the desire for status. Obviously, not everyone can be at the top of the totem pole. In response, you might say it’s only our base desires that are in conflict: there’s no shortage of the truly good things in life, like virtue. To some extent, sure. Virtue isn’t zero-sum. But also among the best things in life are goods like pleasure, knowledge, and achievement, and it is just a fact that these are scarce. We can’t always make everybody maximally happy, and anyone who’s ever organized a class knows that there can be trade-offs between educating one person and educating another.

In the words of Judith Jarvis Thomson, we have some inherently individual interests. And while that might seem like something to lament, it’s also what makes human societies so vibrant, diverse, and dynamic.

Thomson gets the last word (from The Realm of Rights, p. 223).

Given the evil that human beings do to each other, it is no wonder that so many people feel it to be a bad thing in us that we have inherently individual interests. How much kinder bees are to each other! How much more satisfying the life in an ‘organic community’ than the life of alienation in a modern state! The ideal of the hive is seductive and fuels all communitarian ideologies. But the bee-like creatures of our hive-like world are not in fact kind to each other; each is indifferent to the others except insofar as the others are parts of the whole. (It is arguable, in fact, that without inherently individual interests, we would have no personal attachments to individual others, for the possibility of X’s forming a personal attachment to Y rests on the possibility that at least some of Y’s interests will come to be more in X’s own interest than is the interest of the group as a whole—X has to be capable of preferring Y to the group.) And given the creatures we are, the ideal of the state as hive cannot be made real: it is amazing that communitarians have expected otherwise.

You have the right to Subscribe

1

Families rarely come up in Leviathan, though groups do play a role in Hobbes’ argument that “natural condition of mankind” is a “war of all against all.” If all were truly alone, then we’d expect a pecking order to emerge based on differences in strength. But in fact, Hobbes thinks, if someone is stronger than you, you could just rally your “confederates” to team up against him. (Here Hobbes relies on the claim that differences in strength, intellect, etc. aren’t very great.)

For a more systematic look at the role of third parties in conflict resolution, see Mark Cooney, Warriors and Peacemakers. (Cooney’s key idea: third parties are best at resolving conflict when they are slightly above the disputants in social position. If the third party is equal or lower status, they lack the gravitas needed for an authoritative resolution—hence the inability of weak government officials to resolve disputes between early modern aristocrats, who resorted to duels. But if the third party is too far away in status, they won’t understand or be trusted by the disputants—hence the tensions felt in so many countries between police and various minority communities.)

2

Imagine how a rights-free society would have to explain itself to the victim of a rape or shooting:

Look, we agree that your attacker did something wrong, and that you suffered as a result. But let’s not get carried away here: you weren’t the one wronged by this. After all, it is not as though your attacker harmed something of yours—nobody owns their own bodies. And while we will certainly punish your attacker and pay you compensation, this is something we are doing on our own accord, not on your behalf. Again: while we hasten to admit that your body was the location of a wrong, you were not yourself wronged, and so, as an individual, you have no special standing to decide what should happen next.

That said, you are welcome to send us an email, and we will gladly consider your input.

Disgusting.

3

I’m playing this up a bit, but for the record, I think plenty of rights-free moral theories are still eminently worth taking seriously—e.g. certain forms of utilitarianism and Aristotelianism. (Though note that some utilitarians, like J. S. Mill, clearly were rights theorists, and Aristotle himself seems to believe in rights under the heading of “justice.”)

Also, I don’t mean to say that our society, at this very moment, has figured out precisely the optimal suite of rights to give people over their bodies. There’s always room around the edges for disagreement. (What of compulsory vaccines? Human challenge trials, in which people are paid for being injected with pathogens? Hormone therapy for minors?)

But the basic framework—you should get to decide what happens to your body—is essentially correct.

item.title: The culture war is not a conspiracy
item.description: Supply rises to meet demand, and (sadly) the audience demands culture war nonsense.
item.content:encoded:
The GOP is in trouble. Heading into the midterms, gas prices are up ($4.48), Trump’s approval rating is down (37.6%), the trade war with Canada is hurting the economy, and the actual war in Iran is turning out deadlier than we’d been told.

No wonder voters are recoiling. It’s starting to look like this November’s elections will be a true blue wave.

But any truth is liable to be exaggerated. And I came across this semi-viral exaggeration the other day.

Not only is the GOP struggling, says Mike: they lack any grassroots support on big cultural issues. The GOP’s take on gender (e.g.) is really a form of astroturfing, a shiny object to distract the base while the elites rob them blind through old-school trickle down.

I agree that culture wars are, for many people, a distraction from more consequential tax-and-spend issues. But I don’t think Mike’s got the right analysis of culture wars.1 They are not a donor-funded psyop. The truth is far more depressing.

The origins of culture war

Donors have an interest in supplying culture wars, but it’s also the case that audiences demand them.

Think about what kinds of content tends to go viral. It’s not meat-and-potatoes economic stuff—and definitely not tax policy. It’s the culture war: partisan, emotional content that riles people up. The culture war happens largely because it’s what people want to consume.

Subscribe now

I’m not just slinging hunches, by the way. There’s evidence for this in a terrific paper by the economists Shakked Noy and Aakaash Rao (2026). Abstract:

The Business of the Culture War

We link the contemporary American “culture war” to the entry of 24-hour cable news networks, which we find emphasize cultural issues more than the broadcast networks preceding them and far more than political candidates. Estimating viewer preferences using household-by-second data, we show cable news faces a tradeoff: cultural content attracts non-news entertainment viewers while economic content attracts viewers of rival news outlets. Broadcast news and politicians similarly trade off the cultural content that appeals to the politically disengaged against the economic content that appeals to the politically engaged, but we show why cable has the strongest incentives to emphasize culture. In turn, constituencies quasi-randomly more exposed to cable news networks assign greater importance to cultural issues, and politicians run more cultural campaigns.

Noy and Rao’s insight is that media companies and political campaigns are engaged in structurally different competitions. Candidates for office need to win more votes than the opposition, which means that they have an extra incentive to persuade people to switch sides: poaching a voter from the other side is twice as good as turning someone out. Media companies, however, need high absolute numbers of viewers, which means that they’re just as happy poaching a viewer as they are enticing someone to turn on the TV. Culture war content, it turns out, is better at enticing new viewers, whereas plain old econ is better for persuasion. So media companies supply the culture wars that the viewers demand, and the viewers then get riled up and demand more culture-warring from their politicians. This strikes me as a plausible and illuminating take on what’s happening.

The authors also have another paper in the works about culture wars on social media, which will hopefully get published before too long.

The Supply Side of Social Media

…Collecting observational data and conducting experiments with creators and viewers on Instagram, TikTok, X/Twitter, and YouTube, we show that because creators are not paid, content production is dominated by an unrepresentative minority of users who post enviable “lifestyle” content and extreme political content in pursuit of social status and expressive satisfaction. Post-by-post, enviable or extreme posts are not more likely than benign posts to highly engage a given viewer. But the scale at which enviable and extreme content is produced allows platforms to find a greater number of such posts that will appeal to a given user, due to closely matching the viewer’s interests on other dimensions. The prevalence of negative content on social media hence stems partly from platforms’ reliance on cheaply generating scale through status-, emotion-, and conflict-motivated production.

I haven’t been able to read a copy yet, but the abstract passes the smell test, and I find this status-competition hypothesis more plausible than the totalizing “donors did it” narrative.

The Ballad of the Mask-Optional Lesbian Bar

The Boston Globe runs news every day about politics, sports, business, etc. What do you think was their biggest hit this year? A piece on the Fed? Iran? The Red Sox? Nope. It was a story about a lesbian bar that ended its mask mandate and got yelled at on Instagram.

Max Tani of Semafor reports that this story was a record-breaker for the Globe.

The whole article is a cascade of attention-grabbing moments, like this bit from after a disastrous mediation session held at Last Ditch (the aptly named bar):

Noire spends the hours after the meeting posting furious Instagram stories about Matellian and Last Ditch. Matellian (who uses she/they pronouns) had been shedding “WHITE THEY THEM TEARS,” he writes. The bar was not “a safe environment nor interested in revolutionary praxis.”

I’m sorry, but it’s just hilarious that someone calls himself a revolutionary only to spend his time on Instagram whining about imaginary dangers at a lesbian bar. It’s like Che Guevara always said: Safety first!

(And no, I’m not misgendering Mr. Noire, who tells the Globe he “identifies as a gender-expansive lesbian and uses he/him pronouns.”)

See what I mean? I’m sure the Globe’s reporters would prefer to go viral for their reporting on nor’easters, school failures, and state healthcare. But what people actually click on is “drag performer who uses it/its pronouns.” That’s the demand side of the culture war in action.2

Share

Disagreement is real

Not only does the grassroots demand a culture war: they often fight against you.

At the risk of stating the obvious, a lot of voters sincerely disagree with progressives on cultural issues. For example, 2/3rds of the US favor laws against trans women in women’s sports. 2/3rds say it was “mostly a good thing” when SCOTUS struck down affirmative action for university admissions. Just over 2/3rds are opposed to reparations for slavery.3

I don’t want to downplay the influence of donors, and it’s just obviously true that the Republican Party has been using trans sports as a wedge to attack Democrats. But one can acknowledge these facts without exaggerating to the point of self-confusion. Donors aren’t magic. The GOP is flailing in the polls despite crushing in fundraising. And it is difficult to conjure wedge issues out of thin air—often the best wedge is something voters already care about but that hasn’t yet been picked up by politicians.

The fact is, whatever your viewpoint, there are millions of people who disagree with you on just about any given issue. There’s no need to posit a conspiracy of donors hellbent on turning the world against your team.

If you ask me, a better culprit in this instance is unregulated capitalism—specifically, the perfect storm of new tech and for-profit media companies. One annoying thing about capitalist firms is that they tend to innovate whether you want them to or not, and much of the drama in our politics is due to unwelcome innovations in media. 24-hour cable news. Algorithmic feeds. For you. These were great for attracting eyeballs to sell to advertisers, but probably not great for the health of society.4

Share

Wishcasting unanimity

It’s comforting to think that everyone would agree with us on cultural issues if not for the influence of donors. But it just ain’t so. I’m on record as deploring the role of big money in American politics, but even I have to admit that the culture war isn’t a donor-led conspiracy. People really do disagree about this stuff, and these spats are supercharged by for-profit companies lacking in professional ethics.

In fairness to Mike, though, he’s right about one dynamic. There is a well-funded anti-tax coalition in the GOP, and they are in it more for economic than cultural reasons.

But again: there’s no need to exaggerate. Teaming up with cultural conservatives is not the same as astroturfing cultural conservatism into existence. Sincere cultural conservatives exist! I don’t expect them to disappear from American politics anytime soon—though I doubt they’ll be enough of a bulwark to save Trump’s GOP from a midterm backlash.

Thankfully, if there’s one thing President Trump is known for, it’s grace in defeat.

IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS: SUBSCRIBE TO Big iff True

1

Also worth reminding ourselves that not every “culture war” is frivolous—the legalization of gay marriage, e.g., gave important legal rights to gay people and affirmed that they weren’t second-class citizens.

2

As put it last week, “On one hand, I think it’s absurd that this is a story — it’s just some crazy people running a small business badly. On the other hand: It’s all I want to talk about.”

3

Meanwhile, some on the right like Elon Musk say that progressive attitudes towards race are a kind of temporary delusion—a mind virus. This is its own kind of denialism. Many progressives have sincere moral objections to colorblindness and want to live in a country that actively tries to undo the effects of past racism. There is also a significant current of Black Nationalism in the US (which often goes unacknowledged). And of course there are many sincere advocates of a more open immigration policy, a more inclusive policy towards trans people, etc.

4

I agree that certain non-capitalist societies may have had incentives to generate similar technologies (e.g. for the purpose of totalitarian propaganda)—but I don’t think all societies would do this to such an extreme extent.

item.title: From A-bombs to AIs
item.description: Why the nuclear taboo is a great place to start learning about “hostile normative environments,” plus my discussion of AI “doom” with Linch (Forethought).
item.content:encoded:
I’m working on a new project about how to design rules for “hostile normative environments”—such as the Cold War, in which there were fundamental conflicts of interests and ideology between the United States and Soviet Union.

To put it mildly, the Cold War was not a time of “kumbaya.” Indeed, George Kennan famously opened his long telegram from Moscow by arguing that the USSR saw itself as incapable of peacefully coexisting with the US in the long run, quoting a 1927 speech by Josef Stalin to American workers:

In course of further development of international revolution there will emerge two centers of world significance: a socialist center, drawing to itself the countries which tend toward socialism, and a capitalist center, drawing to itself the countries that incline toward capitalism. Battle between these two centers for command of world economy will decide fate of capitalism and of communism in entire world.

From this premise of conflicting visions, Kennan thought, Soviet leaders would conclude that a power struggle was inevitable—and that the US would be naive not to conclude the same.

But despite their hostilities, misunderstandings, and opposing worldviews, the US and USSR succeeded in never declaring war on one another. They also, rather amazingly, defied the expectations of Cold War intellectuals by never launching a nuclear strike, despite having tens of thousands of warheads and several tempting opportunities to use them. If you went back in time to the 1950s and tried to explain to people that the Cold War would end without another Nagasaki—but with both sides’ nuclear stockpiles intact—few among the cognoscenti would believe you. How could clashing superpowers ever hope to cooperate on an issue so vital to their security? This is what led the nuclear strategist Thomas Schelling, in his Nobel Prize acceptance speech, to refer to the era after Hiroshima and Nagasaki as “60 astonishing years.”

We should never forget to be astonished.

Subscribe now

The tradition of the non-use of nuclear weapons, and attitudes of revulsion towards the idea of a nuclear strike, have come to be known as the nuclear taboo. Interestingly, the “taboo” has been denigrated by many influential leaders, including Secretary of State John Foster Dulles and President Dwight Eisenhower. But by the time of LBJ, it was clear to everyone that nuclear weapons were not, as Dulles had hoped, inevitably becoming “conventional.” Quite the opposite: the convention was that nuclear weapons were stigmatized. (For the authoritative story, see Nina Tannenwald’s The Nuclear Taboo, ch. 5.)

The successful stigmatization of nuclear weapons strikes me as one of the most important—and philosophically interesting—achievements of modern civilization. We could learn a lot from the nuclear taboo.

And that is the main idea of my project, titled Priceless Taboos: Moral Theory for Political Practice. The goal is use the nuclear taboo and other case studies as data for coming up with “design principles” for norms that have to operate in hostile normative environments. The term “design principle” comes from Elinor Ostrom’s Governing the Commons, Ch. 3, where she lays out some principles that characterize successful self-governing cooperatives around the world (e.g. resources need clearly defined boundaries, and groups need conflict resolution mechanisms). My hope is to come up with design principles that will not just codify the messy lessons of the 20th century, but also inform the big moral challenges of the 21st—particularly, the need to create workable norms for AI.

AI firms have huge financial interests at stake; China and the US have huge security interests at stake. Different sides have starkly different visions of how AI will impact the global economy—and how it might, or might not, threaten civilization itself. This is exactly what I mean by a hostile normative environment: it’s the kind of scenario where cooperating on basic norms will be difficult. And yet, just as the great powers of the Cold War managed to cooperate on nuclear policy, the powers of the 21st century might be able to cooperate on tech policy. The question is: how?

Share

At any rate, that’s my elevator pitch for Priceless Taboos, themes from which have already been popping up in Big iff True.

For the rest of this week’s post, I wanted to share the transcript of a conversation I had with about AI safety—in particular, about the plausibility of various AI doomsday scenarios. Many thanks to everyone who showed up in the chat and contributed, including the always interesting Simon Goldstein (who is in the AI history books for his experiment at PPA). You’ll also see a bit of Priceless Taboos in action.

The transcript below has been edited for concision and clarity. Video and audio available at this link:

The Linchpin
Livestream Linch: Daniel on how AI takeover could actually happen
I had a great conversation with Daniel Muñoz about possible routes to an AI takeover and/or catastrophe…
Listen now
20 days ago · 5 likes · 1 comment · Linch and Daniel Muñoz

Subscribe now

AI safety and superpersuasion

From AlphaGo to AI safety (0:02 & 10:02)

Daniel: I’m really excited to talk with you today, because I think it’s going to help me settle my own thoughts a bit and try out some of the questions that are nagging me.

First, tell me about how you got into AI.

Linch: I started getting interested in AI safety around 2017. I first heard that DeepMind had this Go program that was ten years ahead of what people predicted. They beat the best European player, which sounds very impressive if you know nothing about Go, but it turns out Europe just doesn’t have any good Go players, even compared to America, certainly not compared to Asia. But within several months, they had a match with Lee Sedol, who was considered at the time the best or second-best Go player of basically all time, and AlphaGo beat him 4–1. Within months of being something like the 300th best player in the world, it became basically number one. A few months after that, a new version played online in secret, without revealing it was an AI, and beat the world’s best players something like 60–0. So it was very clearly an extreme trend.

At the same time, I was reading arguments by people like Nick Bostrom in Superintelligence, and I had friends who thought this was the portent of things to come. Some thought it would look exactly like AlphaGo: deep learning and self-play would get you all the way. Others thought it might look very different. The truth is, it wasn’t exactly like AlphaGo, but it was very close. Large language models are deep learning. There wasn’t that much self-play until recently, but it was extremely close. And I was getting pretty worried. Around 2017 or 2018, I decided that the thing I should eventually work on was AI safety, or reducing existential risk from AI.

Daniel: What have you been doing lately?

Linch: I joined Forethought, a research group that thinks about the impact of AI if things go really fast. How would this go for the future? What are the intelligence explosion dynamics? Can we get robots that automate large parts of the economy?

Personally, I’ve been focusing a lot on AI persuasion. Right now, AIs are more persuasive than people in very narrow lab settings that aren’t very realistic. It seems conceivable that at some point they become more persuasive than people in much more realistic settings: any setting where somebody could talk to you through a laptop, without a physical body, and change your mind, or sell you something, or talk politics. In that situation, you might expect pretty different dynamics than we currently see.

AI persuasion in the lab and in the wild (2:25)

Daniel: Tell me a little bit about AI persuasion. You mentioned there are some experiments that are kind of intriguing.

Linch: In lab settings, both single-turn and multi-turn conversations over 15 minutes, you compare how much people change their minds on political issues when talking to human persuaders, AI persuaders, and very good human persuaders, including expert debaters and professional canvassers. In most of these settings, the AIs are already more persuasive than typical members of even a pretty expert group. That’s been true for at least a year, maybe longer. There were early experiments with GPT-4 getting people to reduce how much they believe in various conspiracy theories, and the reduction was something like 20%. They didn’t compare against a human baseline, but they noted in a footnote that basically no conspiracy intervention of any reasonable size had ever gotten numbers this big.

However, we don’t observe these effects nearly as much in the real world. If AIs were robustly more persuasive than professional humans, you’d expect basically all remote-only sales to be conducted by AI. Any situation where you don’t need face-to-face contact or a physical body, you’d expect to be AI: sales, marketing, ads, diplomacy, scams. AI scams are on the rise, but they’re not huge. It’s not like people are saying, “Oh shucks, I used to work at the scam factory, and now I’m out of a job because the AI took it.”

Daniel: There was a piece in the New York Times about Kenyan contract workers who used to write fake essays. Now fake-essay abundance has been achieved.

Linch: Yeah, there are some domains like that. But in general, I think it’s pretty clear that in real-world persuasion they’re not at the level of humans. Some people argue that’s because of diffusion. That’s not 100% wrong, but I think it’s mostly wrong. I think it’s mostly that the AIs aren’t yet as persuasive in real-world settings that aren’t verbal debates: leveraging relationships, leveraging information about you, getting you to achieve a goal rather than just agree or disagree with propositions.

But it’s possible this increases a lot. Most of the people studying AI misinformation or manipulation imagine it looking very similar to today, just more of it: a flood, people mass-bombarded by nonsense and scam emails. I think very possibly you get both scale and higher quality. First you get to professional human level, where remote-only sales are comparable between humans and AIs. Then peak human level: the best salespeople, Bill Clinton at politics, Kissinger at backroom negotiations. And then maybe it goes further, and that could be pretty interesting and scary.

Easy pickings? (7:24)

Daniel: You mentioned that face-to-face interaction is something humans can do and AIs can’t. I can’t help but point out that face-to-face interaction of certain kinds has been going down. What sociologists call social capital has been cratering in the U.S. since the mid-1960s. Where before you might have hosted a party or gone to the Rotary Club, the Boy Scouts, or a bowling league, now people look things up by themselves on a screen. I wonder if this trend toward isolation makes people easy pickings for persuasion by agents that communicate through their devices, since there’s less interpersonal trust and fewer close connections to keep people grounded in some kind of shared reality.

Linch: Yeah, I do think it’s an affordance. If AIs don’t have physical bodies, which could change, then how much of our economy and politics happens in front of a laptop affects how big a deal this is. It’s similar to cybersecurity. In the 1960s, hacking into a computer gets you almost nothing. Maybe some state secrets, but probably not the nuclear codes, and certainly not blackmail material on random people or their bank account info. By the 1990s, that’s pretty different, and today even more so. Hacking isn’t magic, but it’s much more effective now than it was 30 years ago.

Degrees of threat, not probabilities of doom (15:04)

Daniel: I’d now like to ask about how AI might have a big negative effect. There was an interesting back-and-forth recently between and about how we should talk about the dangers of AI. Pinker thinks just throwing out a probability of doom is unscientific. We shouldn’t treat this as the coming of the end times, but think about it in a cool-headed way and look at it with a chilly eye. Where do you see yourself in that debate?

Linch: For most public discussion, including with lawmakers, to a lesser degree scientists, and certainly journalists, what matters most is degrees of threat more than throwing probabilities around. In grantmaking or certain kinds of research, it’s valuable to know the difference between 1% and 30% and 95%. But in a lot of other contexts, it’s more useful to think in gradations.

The low bar is thinking there’s a threat at all: some chance of a billion or more people dying, the same way there’s some chance of that from asteroids or supervolcanoes. Above that is what I call the moderate position, which was the 2023 CAIS statement, signed by basically the majority of prominent AI scientists, the heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, Bill Gates, and many top AI scientists in China: “Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.” I think that already is enough to motivate a lot of actions we’re not currently taking.

A level above that is a stronger position: the near-term risk of a lot of people dying, or other societal-scale harms from AI, is actually higher than that of nuclear war, natural pandemics, or climate change. My actual belief is a bit higher than that: not just higher than those things, but substantially higher. And you can go higher still: a 90% chance, or “if anyone builds it, everyone dies“ unless we solve a bunch of things first. But in practice, between a 3% chance that a billion people die and a 95% chance that eight billion people die, there are very few things you’d do substantially differently.

Daniel: The way you put it is interesting: what you’d do differently. That sounds like an individual choice, how an individual or a particular leader should respond. But a lot of the issues in AI regulation are going to be collective action problems. But in practice, it’s very annoying to make a giant model. That’s not unlike the nuclear case. You can make a large conventional weapon; it’s just so annoying. And it doesn’t break the taboo, whereas a very small nuclear bomb would. It’s also harder to draw the line by kilotons, because it’s very easy to misestimate the amount. Then, once you have a bunch over the line, what do you do? “According to my analysis, it’s under. According to some other independent analysis, it’s over.” It’s very easy to just creep up each time it’s broken. Whereas if somebody breaks a very clear category of taboo, it’s easier to reinstate. If North Korea launched a nuclear bomb in war, you could censure North Korea, maybe do a land invasion, or you could just say, “Never again will we ever do this,” and maybe it holds up for another 50 years.

But yeah, it’s hard to find sharp lines for AI overall. If you took this concern extremely seriously, you could imagine a line between general AI and specialized AI. Your Waymo is never going to take over the world; it just drives you around. Your highly specialized medical model has some small chance of being used by bad guys for bioterrorism, but it would never initiate that on its own, and maybe we think the medical benefits outweigh the biosecurity downsides. That would be a relatively clear line, though obviously not nearly as good as nuclear versus non-nuclear. But unfortunately, we’re not going to get there. RSI is the line people have talked about.

Daniel: Which is so hard to define. Simon in the chat makes that point: it’s a nice potential line, but how do you define it? And Simon is also pointing out that there’s a bunch of bright lines that have already been blown through: no internet access, no control over autonomous lethal weapons, and so on. To me, this is exactly the problem when it comes to why we’d need to slow down. We have not thought about what the bright lines could be or should be. And nobody is going to respect a bright line that’s yet to be respected. It’s like there are all these pools of a really valuable resource, like fresh water, and we’re polluting them irrevocably before we even think about drawing from them. That’s a real, serious problem. If only we’d watched more Battlestar Galactica, we would have known not to give them internet access.

Last words (1:25:45)

Daniel: I should wrap it up in a minute, but why don’t you take the last words? Is there anything you’d like to leave us with?

Linch: It’s great chatting with you, and thank you to the 50-plus people who came and left great comments in the chat. I’ve been trying to think about how to communicate about these concerns more publicly, so this is pretty helpful, and I hope to write more about this in the future. I think a lot of these questions are uncertain. The technical alignment stuff is pretty uncertain. Whether we should do a pause or a slowdown is uncertain. How all of these laws should be structured is uncertain. But uncertainty doesn’t mean that we should do nothing. Lots of these things are scary, but hopefully manageable, and humanity should try harder. As a member of humanity, I want to do my part, and I hope some of you do as well.

Daniel: Thank you, my fellow try-hard human. I really appreciate your time.

Simon has suggested a potential sequel: maybe a debate about whether super-persuasion is a serious risk. I will say I found your comments on persuasion very interesting and compelling, Linch.

Thank you, everybody, for joining.

item.title: We found two paradoxes
item.description: A new paper in Mind with Daniel Wodak (Penn), ft. an independent discovery by Rachel Higginbotham (USC) in AJP.
item.content:encoded:
I love a good paradox—whether in the form of art, lyrics, books, or Substacks. A lot of my papers try to solve paradoxes in moral philosophy, and my book with Sarah Stroud lays out ethical puzzles by the dozen.

But as much as I like being “part of the solution,” I’ve always wanted to come up with a paradox of my own.1 Well, after many false starts, I finally came up with two!

More accurately: I share custody.

Subscribe now

In 2023, Dan Wodak and I discovered two new paradoxes about duties to self, one of which was independently discovered by Rachel Higginbotham (a brilliant PhD student at USC). My paper with Dan, “Three Paradoxes of Duties to Oneself,” just came out in Mind, not long after Rachel’s paper came out in AJP.2

To set the scene, let me start with an oldie.

Paradox 1: Self-Release

The classic “Paradox of Self-Release” arises from a tension between two ideas about duties.

On the one hand, if you have a duty, that duty has to bind you—constraining what you may do, as jury duty constrains your options for how to spend your day. On the other hand, if someone has a duty to you, then you have the power to release them at will—as when you give a nurse consent to draw your blood.

If you have a duty to yourself, it seems to follow that you are both bound and able to free yourself. But isn’t that incoherent? How could you be “bound” by chains you can remove whenever you like? As Thomas Hobbes put it, “he is free, that can be free when he will.”

Now, personally, I think the way to get out of this paradox is to say that Hobbes is just plain wrong. You can be bound by easily removed chains, or by an easily waived duty. You can be bound even granting that any attempt to violate the duty would fail, because merely intending the act releases you from the duty not to do it. You are bound up until the point when you actually do release yourself.3

That said, hardly anyone agrees with me.4

The more common way to defend duties to oneself is to insist that they’re binding because they’re unwaivable. For example, Kantians often hold that duties to self are “non-contractual,” meaning that they are not the sort of duties created or nullified by consent. Unwaivable duties to self also appear in John Locke’s state of nature, as described in Sec. 6 of the Second Treatise of Government.

But though this be a state of liberty, yet it is not a state of licence: though man in that state have an uncontroulable liberty to dispose of his person or possessions, yet he has not liberty to destroy himself, or so much as any creature in his possession, but where some nobler use than its bare preservation calls for it.

Another source on this—largely forgotten by history until recently—is the early modern novelist Catharine Trotter Cockburn (1743), who was responding to an argument from William Warburton. Warburton had argued that virtue for atheists was paradoxical, because, without God, morality would have to consist in a person obliging himself via his own reason, which doesn’t make sense because (you guessed it) the atheist could release himself from such an obligation at will. Cockburn’s reply, which predates Kant’s Metaphysics of Morals by over half a century, was that atheists can’t actually release themselves. As Jacqueline Broad (2021) explains it:

The power to give up a right applies only when that right is acquired by voluntary compact, not when the right is deduced from the unalterable nature of things. But since a moral obligation is grounded in the essential difference between good and evil, right and wrong, it is not possible simply to withdraw ourselves from an obligation of this kind.

And then there are plenty of modern versions of this move, e.g. Wick (1960).

I used to think the appeal to unwaivable duties was merely unnecessary for defending duties to self. Now I think it’s also insufficient.

Paradox 2: Self-Forfeiture

The problem is that even unwaivable duties to yourself can’t “bind” you, if “binding” implies a possibility of violation.

Suppose you have an unwaivable duty to yourself not to harm yourself—say, by breaking your pinky. Then you break the pinky anyway. This should be exactly the kind of case where it’s possible to wrong yourself. But an extremely common view in moral and political philosophy is that, when you try to violate a duty, people’s corresponding duties to you are forfeit. For example, if you try to break my pinky, I no longer owe it to you not to break yours. (More commonly this is put in terms of rights: if you try to violate my right not to have my pinky broken, you forfeit your right that I not break your pinky.)

Wait a minute. If you’re about to violate a duty to yourself, doesn’t it follow that you forfeit that very duty? If so, then it’s not really possible to violate the duty. And a duty that can’t possibly be violated doesn’t seem very binding.5

This is what Dan and I call the Paradox of Self-Forfeiture—if duties to self can be forfeited, then they can’t be binding. (Rachel makes the same point specifically about the duty not to commit suicide.)

Now, you might try to reply that duties to self are unforfeitable. But there are two problems with this.

First, pretty much everyone accepts something like forfeitability of duties in general. In Sec. 7 of the Second Treatise, Locke asserts that rights can be forfeited (“all men may be restrained from invading others rights”)—immediately after insisting on unwaivable duties to self. Kant talks about “throwing away one’s humanity” by violating duties to oneself, and thereby turning oneself into “a thing”—which seems to imply that one is no longer owed the same duties, i.e. that the duties are forfeit. It would be a bit of a cheat for them to stop believing in forfeitability just to get out of the problem of self-forfeiture.

Second, it’s not really clear why duties to self should be unforfeitable. The usual way to show that forfeiture fails is to show that there’s a failure of either proportionality or necessity. If I’m going to pinch you, I forfeit my right that you not pinch me, but I don’t forfeit my right against much larger harms (like being killed)—that’s proportionality. But even if I’m going to kill you, I don’t forfeit my right against being killed if you can easily stop me through much less harmful means (like merely pinching me)—that’s necessity.

Dan and I agree with proportionality, but we argue that it doesn’t bear on self-forfeiture. If you break your own pinky, the harm to the aggressor just is the harm to the victim, so there’s no disproportionality. (Any harm is proportionate to itself!)

By contrast, we think necessity would bear on self-forfeiture: you don’t need to break your pinky in order to stop yourself from breaking that very pinky—you could just decide not to break it! The problem with necessity is that it’s not a true constraint on forfeiture. If someone tries to attack you, and you respond with (proportionate but) unnecessary harm, you may act wrongly, but you don’t wrong the attacker. Your attacker can’t later demand an apology or compensation. Imagine, for example, a man trying to sexually assault a woman. The woman knows she could either run away or slap the man. I don’t think slapping the man would wrong him. Even breaking the man’s finger wouldn’t wrong him! If the man wanted to keep his rights, he shouldn’t have tried to violate someone else’s. And so it goes with rights against, and duties to, oneself.6

Paradox 3: Inconsistent Forfeiture

Or so I thought it went. Upon closer inspection, the very idea of forfeiting a duty to self appears to make no sense!

Let’s think it through. Say you owe a duty to yourself not to break your own finger. If you break it, you’re violating a duty, which means you forfeit people’s duties to you (self included). But that means you’re not violating any duties after all—in which case, you don’t forfeit any duties after all. But in that case, you are violating a duty, in which case your duty to yourself is forfeit—and so on, ad infinitum!

This is what Dan and I call the Paradox of Inconsistent Forfeiture. It’s a bit like a moral version of the Liar Paradox. Consider the sentence L = “This sentence is false.” If L is true, it must be false (since that’s what L says)—but if L is false, it must be true (since what L says is the case). Similarly: if you violate a duty to yourself, that duty is forfeit—but if the duty is forfeit, you don’t violate it!

In the paper, we call this paradox “Escheresque,” and we canvas a few ways of trying to get out of it. None seems especially promising.

Conclusions

The three paradoxes of duties to oneself are interrelated, but also somewhat independent of each other, in the sense that solving one doesn’t automatically solve the others. For example, you could solve the Paradox of Self-Release by positing unwaivable duties to self, or you could solve the Paradox of Self-Forfeiture by positing unforfeitable duties to self—but neither move solves both. And the Paradox of Inconsistent Forfeiture needs only very minimal assumptions to get going: as long as someone owes a single forfeitable duty to themselves, we can derive a contradiction.

Now for some reflections that aren’t in the paper:

The conclusion I’d like to draw, naturally, is that I was right about everything from the start. After all, one perk of my original solution to the Paradox of Self-Release is that it straightforwardly extends to the Paradox of Self-Forfeiture. Both paradoxes rely on the assumption that duties to self, in order to be “binding,” must be possible to violate. If you reject that assumption (as I do), you solve both at once. But this approach seems to leave us with a great many forfeitable duties to ourselves, which means we run headfirst into the Paradox of Inconsistent Forfeiture!

By contrast, the common solution to the Paradox of Self-Release—viz. the appeal to unwaivable duties—doesn’t help at all with the Paradox of Self-Forfeiture. Perhaps we should extend the solution by saying that duties to self are both unwaivable and unforfeitable. That wouldn’t be the most elegant maneuver, but it does have the virtue of avoiding the Paradox of Inconsistent Forfeiture.

…or does it? Suppose you and I simultaneously attack each other out of the blue. Do we violate our duties to each other not to attack? If so, then it seems our duties are forfeit—but then we don’t violate those duties after all, in which case our duties aren’t forfeit. And so on. This seems just as bad as the original Paradox of Inconsistent Forfeiture, but it doesn’t rely at all on any views about duties to self! (One way out would be to say only one of us forfeits—but which? If it’s me and not you, even though the case is otherwise perfectly symmetric, isn’t that arbitrary?)

In conclusion, I have no idea what to conclude.
