1

Like Horton (2017) and the All or Nothing Problem, Thomson/Foot and the Trolley Problem, or Parfit and the Non-Identity Problem.

I believe Derek Parfit got to Non-Identity first in 1973—11 years before Reasons and Persons made the problem famous. (Though Robert Adams and Thomas Schwartz independently discovered the problem.) Here’s Parfit from “Rights, Interests, and Possible People,” which was written in 1973 and published in 1976.

Consider the following case, which involves two women. The first is one month pregnant, and is told by her doctor that, unless she takes a simple treatment, the child she is carrying will develop a certain handicap. We suppose again that life with this handicap would probably be worth living, but less so than a normal life. It would obviously be wrong for the mother not to take the treatment, for this will handicap her child. And the person-affecting principle tells us that this would be wrong. (Note that we need not assume that a one-month old foetus is a person, for there will be a person whom the woman has affected for the worse.)

We next suppose that there is a second woman, who is about to stop taking contraceptive pills so that she can have another child. She is told that she has a temporary condition such that any child she conceives now will have just the same handicap; but that if she waits three months she will then conceive a normal child. It seems clear that it would be wrong for this second woman, by not waiting, to deliberately have a handicapped rather than a normal child. And it seems (at least to me) clear that this would be just as wrong as it would be for the first woman to deliberately handicap her child.

But if the second woman does deliberately have a handicapped child, has she harmed him-affected him for the worse? We must first ask: “Could he truly claim, when he grows up, ‘If my mother had waited, I would have been born three months later, as a normal child’?” The answer is, “No.”

The problem is that it seems wrong to deliberately have the less well-off child, but it also seems difficult to see what could be wrong about it given that nobody is affected for the worse.

The Trolley Problem’s provenance is complicated, but basically Foot had a trolley-style example in 1967 involving a tram driver, and Thomson coined the “Trolley Problem” and introduced the famous “Bystander at the Switch” example. For details, see Ethical Theory, which has three entries on the Trolley Problem!

For more recent paradoxes, see Zachary Goodsell (2021), “A St Petersburg Paradox for Risky Welfare Aggregation,” and David Builes (2020), “A Paradox of Evidential Equivalence.”

2

The Australasian Journal of Philosophy has published much of the what I call the second wave of work on duties to self, including papers by Tim Oakley (2017), me (2020), Janis Schaab (2021), Paul Schofield (2021), and Yuliya Kanygina (2022)—which are all about the “Paradox of Self-Release.” That paradox got its canonical statement in a short paper by Marcus Singer (1959) in Ethics, which then put out the first wave of papers on the topic. (See Cholbi (2015).)

Between the waves, AJP put out a hidden gem by Nicholas Fotion (1965) and a certified classic by Michael Stocker (1976). Apparently Stocker talked about his paper with Michael Slote, who went on to argue for a similar “Self–Other Asymmetry” in his classic JPhil paper in 1984, in which he didn’t cite Stocker. (“I can only imagine that Slote did not remember these talks,” Stocker [1994] would later say in a grumpy footnote. Slote [1994] replies that Stocker’s argument for the Asymmetry was already present in “Aristotle, Sidgwick, Ross, and Falk,” and that Slote’s contribution was to bring out “the oddness and paradoxical character of the asymmetry…”.)

By the way, Rachel’s paper—“Three Dimensions of Self-Directed Duties”—is only partly about the new paradox. It also has, in my view, the best discussions out there on compensation for self-wronging (an unsolved problem since Baier’s [1958] The Moral Point of View) and the weightiness of duties to self (which I’ve been puzzling over since 2017, when Quinn White asked me about it after a WIP at MIT). See also ’s (2025) excellent new paper on self-blame for self-wronging.

3

I got this idea from G. A. Cohen’s (1996) discussion of Hobbes in “Reason, Humanity, and the Moral Law,” his contribution to Korsgaard’s Sources of Normativity. Cohen’s intro is an all-time favorite.

You might think that, if you make a law, then that law binds you, because you made it. For, if you will the law, then how can you deny that it binds you, without contradicting your own will? But you might also think the opposite. You might think that, if you are the author of the law, then it cannot bind you. For how can it have authority over you when you have authority over it? How can it bind you when you, the lawmaker, can change it, at will, whenever you like?

Now, in that pair of arguments mutually contradictory conclusions are drawn from the selfsame premiss: the premiss that you make the law. So at least one of the arguments is invalid. But, even if they are both invalid, they might still be unignorable, because they might have elements of truth in them. They might be healthy argument–embryos out of which sound arguments could develop. And, whatever else is true, each of the arguments is sufficiently persuasive that, mutually contradictory though they are, each was affirmed in Hobbes’s Leviathan, in much the form in which I just stated them.

For whatever reason, these paragraphs grabbed me when I read them as an undergraduate. I had to know which argument was invalid!

Spoiler: Cohen ends up concluding that the sovereign can be bound by the law he authors—he’s bound until he repeals the law. (Rosati [2011] would later make the same point about self-promises; see also Schaab [2026] on self-binding.)

4

One of several exceptions is my co-author Nathaniel Baron-Schmitt. A bit of background: in January 2015, during our first year of grad school, the two of us pulled an all-nighter talking about duties to self and supererogation—the first time either of us had seriously thought about either topic. Together, we came up with the idea that supererogation (the idea that some good deeds lie beyond the call of duty) emerges from your control over your duties to yourself. At the time, I mistakenly thought we were working out the details of my former teacher Jonathan Dancy’s view. It turns out I was misremembering. It was nobody’s view—though Shelly Kagan (1989) and Paul Hurley (1997) had come up with precursors in the 1980s and 1990s, respectively.

If you’re curious how the view turned out, see “From Rights to Prerogatives” (2020).

5

Though I, personally, would be happy to say that the duty binds you until it’s forfeited.

6

Rachel’s response to the paradox is, interestingly, the opposite of ours. She thinks self-harm violates proportionality, because the harm is significant compared to the total lack of benefit. She also accepts necessity as a constraint on forfeiture—though she thinks some actual cases of self-harm might be proportionate and necessary for preventing future self-harm!

item.title: Why is so much analytic philosophy so boring?
item.description: It doesn’t have to be!
item.content:encoded:
Look, I’m not going to sit here and pretend I don’t love analytic philosophy. I do. I love that we put a premium on clarity. I love that we expect everyone to answer objections from anyone (even if the speaker is a superstar and the objector is a freshman). I love that we aspire to let 1,000 flowers bloom while also shellacking each flower with 10,000 objections. I love that some of us are kooky architects of grand metaphysical systems (like David Lewis) while others are doing spadework on technical problems in logic and probability (like David Lewis).

Subscribe now

However.

I’m pretty sure that anyone who has read a fair bit of analytic philosophy has, at some point, become frustrated with both the style and substance of the enterprise.

For an example of the field’s blandcore aesthetic, consider Robert Shope’s classic 1978 JPhil paper “The Conditional Fallacy.” The paper starts off with a straightforward promise:

Many contemporary philosophers have committed a certain fallacy which, surprisingly, has not yet received a clear description. If one is provided we may be better able to avoid this mistake in the future.

Great! What’s the fallacy? Shope tells us that the “conditional fallacy” is

a mistake one makes in analyzing, defining, or paraphrasing a statement p or in giving necessary and sufficient conditions for the truth of that statement, by presenting its truth as dependent, in at least some specified situations, upon the truth (falsity) of a subjunctive conditional, ∅, of the form: ‘if state of affairs a were to occur then state of affairs b would occur’, when…

One has overlooked the fact that in some of the specified situations the occurrence of certain relations involving factors that are mentioned in p or in the analysans (definiens, paraphrase, or list of necessary and sufficient conditions) is connected either with the occurrence of a or with the absence of a in such a way as to be responsible for a disparity between the truth value of p and the truth value of the analysans (definiens, etc.) in those situations.

“Clear” enough for you?

Just so you know, that abomination is the “succinct” version. The full fallacy is an entire page long and comes with three (3) footnotes.1 (For another example, see the Grice passage in my post on writing.)

Share

A supposed substantive problem

As for the substance of analytic philosophy, there are many complaints to choose from. One recurring gripe is about armchair methodology. An exemplar here is Philip Kitcher’s What’s the Use of Philosophy?, which accuses the field of being out of touch with practical applications. Among analytic philosophers— who are “dominant in the English-speaking world”—Kitcher thinks there is too little interest in real issues and too much idle speculation about the nature of our own concepts, which we’re monomaniacally trying to clarify.

Philosophy’s central task is seen as one of providing analyses of concepts, analyses exact enough to make the concept completely clear.

Now, personally, I don’t find Kitcher’s objection all that worrisome.2

It’s true that there are limits to what you can figure out a priori (that is, without empirical knowledge gleaned from experience, history, science, etc.). Everybody knows you need some real-world knowledge if you want to talk about whether rent control has various economic effects, and whether democracies tend to outperform autocracies in various dimensions. But there are also perfectly legitimate questions that you can ask without getting into the empirical weeds. For example, is it possible to know something if you’re not completely certain of it? Are colors properties of things in the world (like bananas and apples), or of our experiences? Is equality intrinsically good? Is the Liar sentence (“This sentence is false”) true, false, both, or neither? Is there one true logic, or are there multiple legitimate logical systems? Are all necessary truths true by definition, or are there some necessary truths that we have to discover using scientific methodology? (Kripke’s example: “Water = H2O.”)

In addition, it’s just not true that analytic philosophers are primarily out there analyzing concepts. One of the main lessons of analytic philosophy is that such analyses are extremely difficult, if not impossible, so we shouldn’t put too much stock in looking for them.

The most notorious example is the concept of knowledge, the analysis of which was attempted in the voluminous literature on the “Gettier Problem.” The problem begins from the supposedly traditional idea that you can analyze knowledge as justified true belief (JTB)—basically, if you believe something for a good reason, and the belief is true, then your belief amounts to knowledge. Edmund Gettier smashed this analysis with counterexamples so devastating that we now just call them “Gettier cases.” A modern version: I see my neighbors washing an electric car in front of their apartment. I come to believe on that basis that they own an electric car. That belief is justified given what I’ve seen, and it turns out to be true—but only by dumb luck. They were washing someone else’s car as a favor. Their own car (also an electric) is in the shop. Here, my justified true belief fails to be knowledge. In response, would-be conceptual analysts have proposed all kinds of other conditions to supplement the JTB analysis, to which scrupulous epistemologists have responded with ever-more-convoluted counterexamples.

Point being: while there are still some people out there attempting conceptual analysis—sometimes, as in Bernard Suits’ analysis of games, with considerable success—that’s hardly the dominant method of contemporary analytic philosophy.

So what are we doing?

I don’t think there’s just one thing. There are at least three types of projects you can find:

  1. Normative: making arguments about what kinds of beliefs, attitudes, and actions are right, wrong, or rational.

  2. Metaphysical: talking about what it is to be this or that thing (e.g. what is consciousness? what is causation? what is it to be human? what is morality?), or what things are fundamental (e.g. is consciousness nothing over and above certain types of brain activity?) This can be about concepts, or it can be about things in the world.

  3. Applied: asking normative, metaphysical, or interpretive questions that arise organically within particular arts or sciences (e.g. physics, linguistics, psychology, film).

In my view, none of these projects is categorically bad or boring. There are great works of pure metaphysics (e.g. Kit Fine’s “Towards a Theory of Part”), great works of pure normativity (e.g. J. J. Thomson’s Rights, Restitution, and Risk), and great works of “applied” philosophy (e.g. Joe Heath’s Cooperation and Social Justice).

Subscribe now

The real problem

The problem, I suggest, is that analytic philosophers often try to mix projects in an illicit way.

In particular, it’s tempting to base grand conclusions about X on metaphysical musings about X’s nature. For instance, you might try to advocate for some race- or gender-related policy on the basis of a metaphysical claim about what races and genders are. Or someone might try to argue against gay marriage by arguing that marriage—as a matter of its concept or essence—is essentially “aimed” at procreation.

These projects, I concede, are not always doomed to fail. Sometimes there really is a lot of conceptual or metaphysical confusion out there, and clearing it up might help people understand some social or political issue. I’ve even tried my hand at this—see my post from last March, in which I argued that the Trump Administration’s case for striking Iran was partly based on a faulty conception of war.

But such projects are always perilous. If you try to establish non-philosophical points with purely philosophical arguments, you are in serious danger of wasting everybody’s time.

You just can’t make a good normative argument in politics without getting into relevant political and economic facts. No amount of metaphysics will ever establish that inclusionary zoning makes housing affordable. No amount of conceptual tinkering will ever tell us what to do about childhood vaccination, girls’ sports, or immigration policy. If you want to make arguments that are relevant to real-world issues, you are almost certainly going to have to bring in some real-world facts and wisdom eventually. Philosophy is great, but it’s not a cheat code for winning political arguments with zero relevant knowledge.3

(Some years back, there was a book on the epistemology of mathematics that, per one review, “focused throughout” on just one elementary example —“7 + 5 = 12.” Oof. Contrast that with, e.g., the deeply informed work of Bill D’Alessandro.)

A less serious type of failure is when people do quasi-political metaphysics without even trying to connect it to an associated real-world issue. They just analyze “oppression” (e.g.) from a purely philosophical point of view, as if out of professional habit, and hope that the endeavor strikes you as vaguely important, given that the concept features in so many other important debates. Never mind whether those debates need a sharper concept, or whether the sharpening is intrinsically illuminating or worthwhile. The philosopher just sharpens and clarifies for the sake of sharpening and clarifying. I’m tempted to call this cargo cult philosophy.4

Moral of the story: if you want to do philosophy of X (or just contribute to the discourse on X-policy in a relevant way), it’s great to know some philosophy, but don’t be surprised if you have to spend months or years learning about X in itself.

Conclusion

I’m no hater, but even I admit that analytic philosophy has a tendency to go beyond its skis in a way that can be annoying and, yes, boring. The pathology of analytic philosophy is to present itself as making great contributions to topics of importance even where the contributions have little to do with what makes the topic important. At other times, analytic philosophers simply forget to ask whether their topic is of genuine intellectual interest. In either case, the result is a meticulous analysis of that which no one needed analyzed.

Analytic philosophy is at its best when it’s (1) focused on intrinsically interesting intellectual problems, or (2) applied in combination with relevant knowledge. The source of the danger is that relevant knowledge is a huge pain to acquire, and the most interesting problems tend to be buried in massive scholarly literatures. Good analytic philosophy therefore requires (1) becoming an interdisciplinary expert, (2) reading a ton of philosophy—or, if you’re feeling lucky, (3) striking upon an interesting but underappreciated problem. Boring analytic philosophy isn’t inevitable, but it is the path of least resistance.

That’s my objection. Of course, as an analytic philosopher, objections are my preferred means of expressing affection.

So don’t take this the wrong way. ❤️

PS: for more complaining, see David McNaughton’s classic “Why is so much philosophy so tedious?”—which Dave Chalmers once suggested was a corollary of Sturgeon’s Law (“90% of everything is crap”). In grad school, I presented McNaughton’s paper in a reading group (here’s a pdf of my handout), and so many people (Lyndal Grant, Kieran Setiya…) had interesting comments. I came away thinking that we should beware isolated evaluations of papers and books. It’s easy to snipe at “incremental tinkering,” but you can’t really have a functioning academic ecosystem where everyone is trying to do grand projects and nobody is zooming in on the details.

1

In his writing guide, my ANU colleague Al Hájek quotes a wall of Shope-text and asks, “Is he serious?” (Which gets me every time.)

2

Tim Williamson didn’t like that objection, either—thanks to Frank Jackson (another ANU colleague) for reminding me of TW’s review the other day.

3

Again, there are exceptions. Some policies are by their nature so incredibly unjust—like human chattel slavery—that only the slightest dose of empirical reality is needed to establish their injustice.

4

For an illustration, look no further than the immortal JPhil article “Stoppism: Retrospects and Prospects,” an unbearably accurate article on the metaphysics of trains, by the pseudonymous “Myrtle Willoughby.”

Prof. Willoughby begins in media res:

The simplest approach to understanding stoppism is through the answer it gives to that vexed but compulsory philosophical question, “Why are there locals but also expresses?” I am not here concerned with the local/express distinction. I hold that distinction to be exclusive but not exhaustive with respect to trains, and both exclusive and exhaustive with respect to stops. But nothing I defend depends on those views, or on anything beyond the banal claim that the local/express distinction applies first of all to either trains or stops and only later, and in virtue of this prior application, to anything else. Uses such as “express platform” and “local track” undoubtedly occur; any account of the local/express distinction must permit them. But no one seriously contends that these uses are basic, and that local and express trains and stops are to be explained in terms of local or express tracks or platforms.

Thus there are only three serious answers to the vexed but compulsory question: that there are local and express trains because there are local and express stops; or, that there are local and express stops because there are local and express trains; or, that there are local and express trains and stops because of something else altogether. The first is the answer of the stoppists; those giving the second answer are nowadays usually called train-realists. There is no helpful, general term for “Views of the Third Kind,” as they are sometimes called. They come in bewildering variety. Loosely, they can be grouped in two: either they appeal to something “outside the subway,” in which case we stray out of philosophy and into the realms of magic or religion; or they try to account for the existence of local and express trains and stops entirely on the basis of reality “inside the subway.” Views of this last kind are commonly known as “naturalist,” though this term borders on, and very often trespasses into, sheer vacuity.

This passage is, to my mind, almost unbearably painful—and painfully accurate.

item.title: Stop making excuses for scumbag behavior
item.description: We have to start thinking about the long run
item.content:encoded:
In 2026, I’m afraid that we’re all used to low blows in politics. But this week we hit a new low.

In the Ohio governor’s race, Vivek Ramaswamy has taken responsibility for an ad against his opponent Amy Acton (pledging to spend $4 million on it) featuring Acton’s estranged mother Donna Arthur.

Amy has a serious problem. She is a liar. She lies about her past. She says she grew up living in a tent. None of that is true. She’s lied her entire life. My daughter needs help. And she can’t help you if she needs help herself.

But it is just crazy that Ramaswamy would go there. Arthur is not saying that her daughter has misguided political views. She’s disputing Acton’s allegations of child abuse. In particular, Acton claims she was neglected by her mother and raped by her stepfather. Both allegations are credible. When Acton’s stepfather was charged with rape in 1978, while his stepdaughter was just 12 years old, he and Arthur fled the state. The claim about the tent is attested by paperwork from the stepfather’s 1978 arrest, a 1982 police report, and a statement from Acton’s brother.

There’s more, courtesy of PolitiFact:

Pennsylvania court records corroborate that both Donna Arthur and Cledith Arthur were convicted of felony theft by deception in 1996.

Donna Arthur also was convicted of animal neglect in Pennsylvania in 2021 after authorities found cats and kittens in a hot, locked vehicle. The Pennsylvania Superior Court vacated the conviction and sentence in 2023 and remanded the case for further proceedings.

If Ramaswamy had uncovered some hard evidence that Acton had made things up, that would be one thing. But that’s not what he did. The ad is just dirt, apparently for dirt’s sake. It’s giving a convicted felon a national platform to attack the daughter she allegedly abused. (Also, the woman’s kittens were found in a hot car. I’m supposed to take her word that she wasn’t neglectful?)

Initially, Ramaswamy didn’t stand by the ad—when it went viral, there was no disclosure of who had been backing it. Ramaswamy only admitted to it later.

Subscribe now

Here is Acton’s response:

There has been a significant backlash, I am happy to say, including among Republicans. “I don’t have to agree with Amy Acton’s politics to believe that exploiting someone’s childhood trauma is wrong,” said Lydia Mihalik, Director of Ohio’s Department of Development. Meghan McCain called it “a dastardly ad. It never should have been created. Shame on whatever consultant firm created this.” Former SC Governor Nikki Haley said of Ramaswamy “he’s a bad guy. It’s a shame he continues to get away with it.”

Etc.

But for anyone keeping count, this is 2026. So I shouldn’t be surprised to hear this from the Vice President of the United States:

I’ll be honest with you, whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern. What is my concern is who is going to govern the next generation of American government.

I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America.

This is debased stuff. What can’t you justify by that logic?

Worse, Vance is posturing as the adult in the room: “Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts.”1

Subscribe now

Fine, I’ll focus on substance

What are we to make of Vance’s statement? I obviously disagree, but prima facie he has a point. Sometimes, the political stakes of winning an election do seem to matter more than “playing nice.” In fact, there’s a sense in which this is generally true, at least in major elections where you might make a big difference. Isn’t it a kind of false equivalence to treat minor moral principles as being on a par with big-time political stakes?

But dirty politics isn’t just a picayune one-off, with moral costs for this or that individual. When you hit below the belt, you are punching one guy, but you are also cheapening the significance of the belt for everyone and all time. Crossing a moral boundary in plain sight tends to smudge the line, which invites more crossings, which leads to more smudges. The only way to prevent a herd of opportunists and imitators from wiping the boundary out completely is to treat even the first transgression as unacceptable. And the best way to prevent a single line-crossing from starting a pattern is to get the transgressor to bend the knee and atone.

Something similar can be said in favor of the rules for war. Beating the Nazis in WWII was, considered in isolation, obviously more important for the Allies than following every law of war to a T. You might conclude that the Allies should be willing to bend or even break the rules. But if you make a habit out of that kind of “whatever it takes” reasoning, you will very quickly find yourself in a world where POWs are slaughtered, chemical and biological weapons are on the table, and communication between opposing powers breaks down. Think about how corrosive it would be for opposing powers to kill each other’s envoys, for example. If you just think about this as a harm to the envoy, then you can come up with a tough-minded rationale for doing it when it affords some military advantage. But this is a disastrous policy in the long run. How can you negotiate if there’s no safe way to communicate? How do you rebuild those bridges once they’re burned?

When you think of human society in the long run, morality has a way of seeming much more important and fundamental. One-off tradeoffs that look rational in the moment can easily cascade into feuds and disasters. In the long run, it pays to be more absolutist about certain bright moral lines (e.g. the boxer’s belt), even though absolutism otherwise can seem like irrationality—like tradeoff denialism. But the opposite attitude—the willingness to trade off anything in the name of short-term victory—is itself a kind of denialism, a denial of the ramifications our actions have over time and across populations.

The short-sighted, small-minded opportunism of Ramaswamy’s hit could only seem beyond reproach to someone with a short-sighted, small-minded interpretation of the human condition. As if we weren’t part of something that was here before us, and that will outlast us. As if we could just hit below the belt, over and over, blatantly and for the barest of reasons, and expect belts to still mean something in the future.

Last words go to Edmund Burke.

Compute your gains: see what is got by those extravagant and presumptuous speculations which have taught your leaders to despise all their predecessors, and all their contemporaries, and even to despise themselves, until the moment in which they became truly despicable.

From Reflections on the Revolution in France, p. 124.
